articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro herda doadores do pai; Lula mantém aliados do governo | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento do G1 mostra que a maioria dos repasses para os candidatos à Presidência pelo PL em 2022 e 2026 veio de empresários do agronegócio; petista manteve entre os financiadores pessoas que integram ou são próximas do governo federal.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro concentra repasses do agronegócio e empresários, enquanto Lula mantém financiadores ligados ao governo federal em sua campanha.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula em entrevista com Renata Lo Prete — Foto: Globo/ Manoella Mello

Mais de um terço dos doadores de campanha do candidato a presidente de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) financiaram também a candidatura do pai dele, Jair Bolsonaro (PL), nas eleições de 2022. Já Lula (PT) reteve oito financiadores do pleito anterior, que representam 1,4% de todas as pessoas físicas que enviaram recursos à campanha do petista neste ano.

No caso do candidato do PL, dezenove doadores recorrentes fizeram depósitos acima de R$ 100 mil. Destes, treze fizeram as doações depois do primeiro turno das eleições, ou seja, após 4 de outubro. Flávio ficou à frente de Lula nas urnas no primeiro turno. A maioria desses doadores são empresários, presidentes de empresa e produtores e executivos ligados ao agronegócio.

Os maiores aportes, de R$ 500 mil a R$ 1 milhão, vieram de Alexandre Grendene Bartelle, empresário bilionário e cofundador da fabricante de calçados Grendene; Fernando de Castro Marques, presidente da farmacêutica União Química; e Gilson Lari Trennepohl, dono da Stara, uma das maiores empresas de máquinas agrícolas da América Latina.

Do lado de Lula, os oito doadores recorrentes têm relações próximas ou são integrantes do governo. A lista inclui nomes como Celso Amorim, assessor especial para assuntos internacionais; Aloizio Mercadante, presidente do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e Miriam Belchior, ministra da Casa Civil. As doações variam, ao todo, de R$ 1 mil a R$ 27 mil.

As informações são de um levantamento feito pelo g1 com base nos dados disponíveis no portal DivulgaCand do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). Os registros de doações de pessoas físicas às campanhas fazem parte da prestação de contas dos candidatos, que ainda é parcial. Ou seja, a lista de doações de cada campanha em 2026 ainda pode ser atualizada com novos recebimentos.

Qualquer pessoa física pode apoiar financeiramente candidatas, candidatos ou partidos políticos. As doações devem ser feitas de forma identificada e rastreável. A doação por parte de empresas é proibida.

O levantamento do g1 não inclui os valores arrecadados por meio de vaquinhas eleitorais, já que esses recursos são registrados no TSE de forma agrupada, em nome das empresas responsáveis pela intermediação do financiamento coletivo, e não como doações individuais de cada apoiador.

A prestação de contas completa para o primeiro turno deve ser encaminhada à Justiça Eleitoral até 3 de novembro, enquanto informações sobre o segundo turno podem ser enviadas de 26 de outubro até 14 de novembro.

Veja detalhes sobre quem são os financiadores recorrentes:

Flávio recebeu doações de 462 pessoas físicas diferentes. Destes, 161 também doaram para a campanha de Jair Bolsonaro em 2022. Isso significa que um terço das pessoas físicas que enviaram dinheiro à campanha de Flávio fizeram o mesmo com o pai dele.

Em 2022, Jair Bolsonaro foi derrotado nas urnas por Lula. Naquele ano, Jair recebeu financiamento direto de mais de 392 mil pessoas.

No caso de Flávio, dezenove dos doadores recorrentes fizeram depósitos acima de R$ 100 mil. Destes, treze fizeram as doações depois do primeiro turno das eleições. A maioria desses doadores são empresários, presidentes de empresa e produtores e executivos ligados ao agronegócio.

Alexandre Grendene Bartelle, empresário bilionário e cofundador da fabricante de calçados Grendene: doou R$ 1 milhão para Flávio em 2026 e R$ 1 milhão para Jair em 2022. Fez o repasse para Flávio depois do primeiro turno.

Fernando de Castro Marques , presidente da farmacêutica União Química: doou R$ 500 mil para Flávio e R$ 12 mil para Jair. Fez o repasse para Flávio antes do primeiro turno.

Até o momento, Lula recebeu doação direta de 571 pessoas físicas. No pleito anterior, em 2022, teve 139 doadores diretos.

Os oito financiadores que o presidente manteve em sua campanha de reeleição têm laços com o governo. A lista inclui ex-ministros, ex-integrantes do governo Dilma, pesquisadores, secretários executivos e assessores especiais. As doações variam de R$ 1 mil a R$ 27 mil.

Os doadores novos de Lula têm perfil semelhante ao dos recorrentes. Como mostrou o g1 , aparecem na prestação de contas contribuições de pessoas próximas ao governo atual e também serviços prestados (casos em que o valor declarado corresponde a um serviço oferecido à campanha, e não a uma transferência de dinheiro).

Entre os doadores estão Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, um dos coordenadores da campanha, e Luiz Marinho, atual ministro do Trabalho e Emprego.

A TV TEM realiza, entre os dias 26 e 29 de outubro, o Upfront 2027 , evento voltado a anunciantes e agências de publicidade para apresentação das novidades da programação e das oportunidades comerciais da emissora para o próximo ano.

Com alcance em mais de 370 municípios paulistas, o equivalente a cerca de 60% do território do estado, a afiliada da Globo destaca a força da comunicação regional como estratégia para conectar marcas ao público do interior paulista.

Durante os encontros, serão apresentadas possibilidades de inserção publicitária na programação da emissora e em suas diferentes plataformas de mídia.

TV TEM lança Upfront 2027 para anunciar novidades — Foto: Divulgação/TV TEM

A proposta do Upfront 2027 é aproximar empresas e consumidores por meio de soluções de comunicação alinhadas às características e aos interesses da audiência regional.

Segundo o diretor comercial da TV TEM , Itamar Ferrucci, o evento representa uma oportunidade para que as marcas planejem com antecedência suas ações de comunicação e ampliem o potencial de resultados.

“O Upfront da TV TEM é o momento de antecipar o planejamento, construir oportunidades e potencializar os resultados para o próximo ano. Quem se antecipa tem acesso a condições comerciais diferenciadas, prioridade nos projetos especiais e mais oportunidades de conectar sua marca à audiência em todo o nosso ecossistema de mídia”, afirma.

articles.title: Justiça nega presença de Marcola em júri por assassinato de PM por risco à segurança e de fuga | G1
articles.standfirst: A sessão do Tribunal do Júri está marcada para os dias 11, 12 e 13 de maio de 2027. Com a decisão, o líder do PCC vai acompanhar o julgamento e ser interrogado por videoconferência, diretamente da unidade prisional.
articles.summary: A sessão do Tribunal do Júri está marcada para os dias 11, 12 e 13 de maio de 2027. Com a decisão, o líder do PCC vai acompanhar o julgamento e ser interrogado por videoconferência, diretamente da unidade prisional.
articles.body:
Marco Willians Herbas Camacho, o Marcola, foi transferido para a Penitenciária 2 de Presidente Venceslau (SP) em 2014 — Foto: Arquivo/TV Fronteira

A Justiça de São Paulo negou, por razões de segurança pública e pelo risco de resgate dos presos, o pedido para que Marcos Willians Herbas Camacho, o Marcola, apontado como líder do PCC, acompanhe presencialmente seu julgamento por homicídio e tentativa de homicídio de policiais militares.

Os crimes ocorreram em Jundiaí, no interior de São Paulo , em 12 de maio de 2006, durante os episódios que ficaram conhecidos como "Crimes de Maio". As vítimas foram os policiais militares Nelson Pinto e Marcos Henrique dos Santos Moraes.

O julgamento pelo Tribunal do Júri está marcado para os dias 11, 12 e 13 de maio de 2027. Com a decisão, Marcola deverá acompanhar a sessão e ser interrogado por videoconferência, diretamente da unidade prisional onde está detido.

Além dele, respondem ao processo Júlio César Guedes de Moraes e Marcos Paulo Ferreira Lustosa que também vão participar do júri popular por videoconferência. As defesas dos três acusados haviam solicitado que eles participassem presencialmente da sessão.

A decisão foi proferida em 22 de outubro pelo juiz Gustavo Celeste Ormenese, da 1ª Vara do Júri do Foro Central Criminal de São Paulo.

O magistrado considerou pareceres contrários ao deslocamento dos presos emitidos pela Penitenciária II Maurício Henrique Guimarães Pereira, em Presidente Venceslau, e pela Coordenação-Geral de Classificação e Movimentação de Presos do Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública.

Segundo a decisão, o transporte dos réus entre as unidades prisionais e o fórum representaria risco concreto à ordem pública. O juiz citou a possibilidade de resgates, emboscadas em rodovias e confrontos armados durante o trajeto, além da necessidade de mobilizar um grande contingente policial para realizar a escolta.

O magistrado também afirmou que o deslocamento exigiria a retirada de um número expressivo de policiais militares e penais de suas atividades regulares. Por isso, determinou que os réus participem de toda a sessão do júri e sejam interrogados pela plataforma Microsoft Teams.

Em nota, o advogado Bruno Ferullo Rita, que representa Marcola, lamentou a decisão e afirmou que a presença física do acusado diante dos jurados é uma expressão da garantia constitucional de plenitude de defesa.

A defesa argumentou que a videoconferência é uma medida excepcional e que sua adoção exige fundamentação concreta, não bastando, segundo o advogado, a alegação de riscos genéricos relacionados à custódia em presídios de segurança máxima.

O advogado também citou um caso semelhante, no qual outra Vara do Júri do mesmo fórum solicitou a apresentação presencial de um preso custodiado em penitenciária federal de segurança máxima. Segundo a nota, a Justiça Federal autorizou o pedido e o Sistema Penitenciário Federal confirmou a realização da escolta.

A defesa informou que vai recorrer da decisão e adotar as medidas cabíveis para garantir a participação presencial de Marcola no julgamento.

articles.title: Blanche: DOJ could block election certification in ‘doomsday scenario’
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche left the door open on whether the Department of Justice (DOJ) would intervene in states’ midterm elections verification process...
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche left the door open on whether the Department of Justice (DOJ) would intervene in states' midterm elections verification processes, telling reporters Thursday there are hypothetical "scenarios" in which it could block the certification of votes.

"Yes, of course there's scenarios that we can all come up with hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario for example, right?" he said. "So, I don't think it's proper to make any kind of conclusory statements about what's going to happen in the future, because I have no idea what's happening in the future."

Blanche added the DOJ has no intention "to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process."

"There's no circumstances that we would ever do that," he continued. "Of course I'm not going to say that. But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not, no, not at all."

Blanche said earlier this month the DOJ plans to send 1,000 election monitors to polling places in every state on Election Day. At the time, he told Fox News anchor Shannon Bream the department's presence would serve to ensure federal law is properly enforced, adding the government has been monitoring elections since the 1960s.

During the Fox interview, Blanche went on to accuse Democrats of "fearmongering" by claiming the DOJ is trying to intimidate voters.

On Tuesday, Democratic leaders and election groups filed a lawsuit against President Trump and the DOJ, accusing the administration of " threats and intimidation " ahead of Election Day — pointing to its efforts to push states to identify and remove suspected non-U.S. citizens from voter rolls and threats of criminal prosecution against election officials who refuse to comply.

DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told The Washington Post on Wednesday that "ensuring that only eligible citizens vote and that every lawful ballot is counted a requirement of federal law."

The lawsuit specifically cites the DOJ's demand for California officials to set aside ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) identified as noncitizens. It also alleged the administration's threat to imprison state and local election officials violated the Voting Rights Act.

The DOJ sued California last week after giving its officials 48 hours to compare DHS's list of 20,000 names to the state's voter rolls. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) slammed the lawsuit, saying the Golden State's elections "are NOT Donald Trump's to control."

On Monday, the DOJ announced 28 alleged non-U.S. citizens in California were charged in connection with illegal voting. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said all of the 28 "defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week."

Trump, who has long held immigration as a central issue over both of his presidencies, has frequently made unsubstantiated claims surrounding noncitizens voting in U.S. elections and alleged the practice plays a role in voter fraud in Democratic states.

articles.title: Trump praises Ramaswamy ad as some GOP critics speak out
articles.summary: "Who wouldn't use such an Ad?" President Trump wrote. "I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'"
articles.body:
Washington — President Trump on Thursday praised the "very powerful ad" Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is running featuring the estranged mother of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, after the ad drew pushback from some Republicans like Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine.

Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social that he suggested Ramaswamy keep the ad up, saying the press is "trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it's so good!"

The ad , which first circulated on social media on Monday and is now television, features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who called Acton a "liar" and sought to undermine her credibility. Acton's campaign condemned the ad, and her brother, Philip Stearns, called it a "despicable low."

According to court documents provided by the campaign, Arthur's now-deceased husband was charged with raping Acton, which she said occurred when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea and left the area while out on bond; the case never went to trial.

DeWine on Thursday said he thought the Ramaswamy campaign should take the ad down . "It's wrong to run this ad," the Ohio Republican told reporters. "I would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take this down." DeWine did not rescind his endorsement.

But Vice President JD Vance and now Mr. Trump are defending the ad and using it to criticize Acton.

"Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse," Mr. Trump wrote in his social media post. "The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad.' Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."

In his post, Mr. Trump did not mention why Acton and her birth mother are estranged, or any of the family's backstory.

Shortly after his post, on the White House South Lawn, reporters told Mr. Trump the backstory — that Acton's mother stayed married to the man charged with raping her. CBS News senior White House reporter Weijia Jiang asked the president why anyone should listen to what the estranged mother has to say.

"Well I know nothing about it," the president responded. "All I know is the mother said very bad things about Acton, who I guess is running for governor against Vivek. And all I can say is Vivek is great. And I know one thing, if my mother said bad about me, it would be a major news story, that's for sure. So I don't know what it is, but I guess the mother said very bad things about the one who's running for governor. And I think you have to say that seriously."

"I'm defending it because I know that if that ad were about my mother, you would love it, you would love every inch of it," Mr. Trump added.

In his Truth Social post, the president specifically went after DeWine.

"Our RINO Governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, who I unfortunately helped get elected years ago, when he was losing by 16 points prior to my doing a Rally for him was, as usual, disloyal to the Republican Party," Mr. Trump wrote. "He strongly suggested that Vivek should, 'take down the Ad.' He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing. I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up..."

Mr. Trump added he only wishes the "mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse."

"Who wouldn't use such an Ad?" Mr. Trump wrote. "I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'"

Mr. Trump continued to defend the ad during a rally in Iowa late Thursday. He said he advised Ramaswamy that "you gotta ride with it," later adding: "Leave it up, and look upstairs and say, 'Thank you God, very much.'"

Vance, too, defended the ad, saying Republicans who have criticized it should "stop whining."

Ohio Republican Sen. John Husted, who is running for reelection, said he "would not have run that ad."

Outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina called the ad the "most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season."

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, a Republican, told a local ABC station he "probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision."

Acton's brother said earlier this week it's "not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point."

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

articles.title: Trump's MAGA faithful send warning to Republicans ahead of high-stakes midterm elections
articles.summary: Trump supporters at his Sioux City rally back Republicans but voice growing frustration over high prices, the Iran war and Election Day turnout.
articles.body: SIOUX CITY, Iowa — President Donald Trump's loyal base of supporters still have his and Republicans’ back in Iowa, but some are growing concerned over lingering issues, like the economy and gridlock in Congress, as Election Day nears. Trump and Republicans ran on a platform of lowering inflation, halting "forever wars" and repairing an economy that they say was wrecked by former President Joe Biden and his administration. But prices are still high, and the war in Iran is still ongoing, causing a spike in fuel prices that have stuck around heading into Nov. 3. Outside of Trump’s rally in Sioux City, Iowa, where the president was set to rile up support for Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, in a tightening Senate race against Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, his supporters who spoke with Fox News Digital still backed Republicans but expressed hope that change would soon come. VOTERS PREPARE TO WEIGH-IN ON TRUMP'S ECONOMY AS COSTS CONTINUE TO SURGE Beth Fitzl, an Iowa voter, said of Trump that she didn’t "agree with everything he does, but in the end, he's here for us." "This is the way I see it," Fitzl told Fox News Digital. "He's like the Packers, OK? They may be getting in deep, but they always pull it off in the end, and I truly think he's going to do something to turn it around. I really think he's going to pull something to turn it around." Chuck Jones, a veteran and Purple Heart recipient who made the trek from Minnesota for the Iowa rally, was frustrated about the divisive, tribal nature of politics. He told Fox News Digital that "these politicians, they're fighting for one thing on one side, and other people are fighting for something on the other side, but there's nobody sitting at the table in the middle." TRUMP VOTERS REVEAL THEIR BIGGEST FEAR HEADING INTO MIDTERMS — AND IT'S NOT RISING PRICES When asked if Republicans and Trump needed to do something different should they hold onto control of Washington, D.C., after the election, Jones said, "Well, I think it's time that we're going to have to show some difference, because people aren't happy with the way things have been in the last few years." "And we're going to have to do something about it and decisively show the American public that you can get it done and get it done correctly," he said. "They're going to have to work together instead of fighting each other." Hinson’s race is one of six toss-ups that Republicans in the Senate are trying to hold onto. She and Turek are vying for Republican Sen. Joni Ernst’s seat after she opted to retire from the upper chamber last year. Their race, like others during this cycle, has become surprisingly close, given that Trump won the state in 2024 by roughly 13 points and has won it each time he’s been on the ballot. THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES Dawn Stanley, an Iowa voter who has voted for Trump in each of the last three elections, still planned to support him and Hinson. She told Fox News Digital that Turek hadn’t "showed up" for Iowa and noted that he’d been absent from the state legislature "42% of the time" — Turek missed 261 votes between January and May of this year while on the campaign trail. Still, her biggest frustration with Republicans was their inability to pass the SAVE America Act, voter ID and election security legislation that has been consistently blocked by Senate Democrats. "I really do think it comes down to the SAVE Act," Stanley said. "I really do, because we can't have all these Democrats in there and bringing over all these illegals who are going to vote for those people and have chaos. That's what it is." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The United States is in chaos and I really believe it's because of the illegals and the Islamic terrorists that are coming over," she continued. "And just look at what's going on in France. I mean, it's terrible. And I don't want that for our country, and that's what Trump can stop. And that's why we need to bring in all the conservatives that we can." Others were concerned about Democrats regaining power and feared that Republicans may not show up on Nov. 3 to support GOP candidates. "We need to get the people out to vote," Kurt, who traveled from South Dakota for the rally, told Fox News Digital. "Republican people need to get out the vote. They stay home too much. This is a war to be won with the Left, as far as I'm concerned."

articles.title: Antifa supporter charged with stealing GOP campaign signs in NY race to replace Stefanik
articles.summary: An Antifa member was allegedly caught on video stealing Anthony Constantino's campaign signs in the NY-21 race to succeed Elise Stefanik in Congress.
articles.body: A New York man was arrested after he was allegedly captured on video stealing campaign signs belonging to Republican congressional candidate Anthony Constantino while driving his employer’s vehicle. Josef Marris was charged with two counts of criminal possession of stolen property, according to the Essex County Sheriff’s Office. He was also fired from East Branch Organics, according to Constantino’s campaign. Constantino, who is running in New York’s 21st Congressional District, said the alleged thefts were intended to intimidate his supporters. TRUMP ENDORSES STICKER MULE CEO WHO BATTLED OFFICIALS OVER 100-FOOT PRO-TRUMP SIGN FOR STEFANIK'S HOUSE SEAT "My campaign has lost more than $100,000 to sign theft and vandalism," Constantino told Fox News Digital. "There are now multiple attempts to intimidate my supporters by people who are clearly pro-crime and pro-violence. The media needs to stop pretending this is a both-sides problem." Constantino’s campaign alleged that Marris carried out the thefts on behalf of Democratic candidate Blake Gendebien. Gendebien’s campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY Constantino also criticized Gendebien in a post on X, writing that the Democrat "is surrounded by FAR LEFT EXTREMISTS." WE NEED TO TALK TO COMMUNISTS BECAUSE THERE IS SO MUCH THEY NEED TO LEARN Marris has described himself as a communist and an Antifa supporter, according to social media posts reviewed by Fox News Digital. In April 2023, he posted an image of the three-arrow symbol, which has historically been associated with several socialist and anti-fascist movements. The symbol alone does not establish that Marris is a member of Antifa or that Gendebien’s campaign had any connection to the alleged thefts. THE BLUE WAVE LOOKS REAL UNTIL YOU LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER The incident comes as Gendebien leads Constantino in a closely watched race to succeed retiring Rep. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y., in the 21st Congressional District. articles.title: What Democrats would do about Gen Z’s housing crisis if they win Congress
articles.summary: Generation Z wants legislation that targets affordability and housing costs. Democrats think they can do it better than Republicans. articles.body:
Generation Z wants legislation that targets affordability and housing costs. Democrats think they can do it better than Republicans.

About two-thirds of young adults struggle to cover housing costs. And recent housing numbers aren’t promising, either: Single-family housing starts and building permits, a measure of future construction, fell 4.56 percent and 4 percent in September, respectively, per the U.S. census.

The National Association of Home Builders also released an October survey on homebuilder sentiment on Tuesday, which came in at the lowest level in 14 years.

Over the summer, Congress signed a sweeping housing package into law with overwhelming bipartisan support, driven by Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Tim Scott (R-S.C.) and Reps. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) and French Hill (R-Ark.).

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act was the most significant legislation on the subject to pass in decades, with 45 different provisions accrued from different lawmakers’ bills across both chambers that made it easier to build new housing and pushed against private equity firms buying up single-family homes.

But other factors are making it more expensive to build homes, including the tariff battle with Canada and the war in Iran, which has led to higher energy prices and, indirectly, rising inflation and interest rates.

All of that may put a damper on the bill’s impact.

Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), the sole Gen Z member of Congress, told The Hill that housing will be a top priority for House Democrats, should they retake the lower chamber.

“The first thing we have to do is greatly expand the inventory of affordable housing,” Frost said, pointing to block grants, like the Community Development Block Grant Program, and other things to “incentivize local governments that push the production of affordable housing.”

The Florida congressman added that more housing isn’t the only solution — Congress needs to address ways renters are “taken advantage of via junk fees and credit scores being used as the end-all bill to decide whether or not they can rent,” Frost said.

But he also wants to make homeownership more in reach for younger Americans. The average age of first-time homebuyers has skyrocketed well beyond the age of Gen Zers.

“If we can slash it by 12 years in the next 4 years, I think that will be a really good start,” he said.

When asked if collaboration between Democrats and Republicans is possible on this issue, the congressman had mixed feelings.

“I think there’s going to be some bipartisanship on the building aspect of things. I think a lot of that falls apart when we talk about the cost associated with it,” he said.

Warren told The Washington Sun that a ROAD to Housing 2.0 bill is underway, “with lots of room to expand.”

She also said if Democrats take Congress in 2026, they would push for new housing legislation focused on “starter homes, renters and manufactured housing.”

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) told The Hill in a statement she believes “too many young people are working hard and still finding that rent takes too much of their paycheck to get ahead.”

“We need to make housing more affordable so young people can build a future, save for a home, and have the opportunity to thrive,” Klobuchar continued.

Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), vice chair of the Congressional Renters Caucus, said she has pushed for federal housing reforms, but many bills under the current Republican-majority Congress have been shot down.

“With a Democratic majority, we can and must provide essential support for young adults amid Trump’s housing and affordability crisis,” she said in a statement to The Hill.

Her proposed legislation includes help for first-time, first-generation homebuyers; protection against illegal evictions; and safeguarding tenants’ right to stable and affordable housing.

Lucas Holtz, a senior political adviser at Third Way, a Democratic, D.C.-based think tank, says young voters who complained about Democrats and the economy in 2024 are now raising the same concern with the Trump administration.

“They are pissed, and Republicans promised they would lower costs,” Holtz said.

Third Way has focused on why young men — a key demographic for President Trump in 2024 — believe the president has failed them.

Research shows that 61 percent of young men say Trump is failing to fulfill his campaign promises, including a quarter of young Republican men.

Meanwhile, Democrats are running on housing and “making life more affordable” campaigns, Holtz said, which stick out to Gen Zers.

If Democrats were to take control of Congress, Holtz believes they would focus on ending Trump’s tariffs, especially on lumber and housing materials, to make housing more affordable.

Holtz says Democrats such as Georgia Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani stick out to Gen Zers. He believes young adults’ drift toward democratic socialism is a result of tightening economic conditions.

When considering the rise in democratic socialist supporters, “it is not an endorsement of socialism, but a rejection of the current status quo of the economic system,” Holtz said.

“The left is over-performing in all of the polls and are making deep red states and districts competitive for one simple reason, because they understand voter concerns in their districts,” he added.

State Rep. Manny Rutinel, who is running for Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, told The Hill that he was one of few renters in the Colorado House.

Should he win the seat in November, Rutinel also said he plans to target Trump’s “corrupt, chaotic tariffs,” that “need to end immediately.”

“I know the struggle that Gen Z and young adults are enduring because, as a 31-year-old, I am going through the same hardships and fears of never being able to buy a home,” he said.

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

articles.title: Trump ties big promises to GOP midterm election wins
articles.summary: President Trump’s growing list of promised “goodies” if Republicans win has become more niche the closer the country gets to the midterm elections. Trump and the GOP are hoping his big promises to voters will get them out to the polls on Election Day in less than two weeks. From payment of a $5,000 dividend to…
articles.body:
President Trump’s growing list of promised “goodies” if Republicans win has become more niche the closer the country gets to the midterm elections.

Trump and the GOP are hoping his big promises to voters will get them out to the polls on Election Day in less than two weeks.

From payment of a $5,000 dividend to all Americans if Republicans win to dangling investments and settlements, these Trump promises have become a staple at his campaign stops.

The efforts have drawn skeptics who question if Trump’s big promises will work, are legal or will even happen.

“The problem that Trump faces right now is that no one believes him on ending the war. On lowering prices. On giving away money. None of it,” said a former White House official. “I’m not sure if it is hurting Republican candidates, but it certainly isn’t helping.”

Trump has doubled down on some promises. He wrote in a Truth Social post last month, “When I say something, I mean it!” in regard to the dividend checks.

“I think there’s a fine line with going in and promoting what you’ve done for a district or for a state or what’s on the horizon for a district or for a state versus having it appear as a quid pro quo or worse,” said one Republican strategist.

“We’ll just see if that’s enough to swing them or if they’re just going to focus back and bounce back to the economy and general corruption issues that are influencing them anyway,” the strategist said, adding, “personally for me, I don’t like it.”

Michael Kang, a law professor at the Northwestern Pritzker School of Law, said it’s not bribery or a vote buying scheme.

“There’s no vote buying problem with that,” he said. “That’s just like saying, if you vote for us, we’re going to pass tax cuts and everyone’s going to get money back.”

The White House dismissed any criticism of the promises.

“The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump: when he pledged to create the historic Trump Accounts, lowered prescription prices with Most Favored Nations, secured the border with no crossings, cleaned up our streets, ended taxes on tips, grew real wages, renegotiated broken trade deals, and reshored key manufacturing back to the United States,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement.

Trump promised the $5,000 “Trump dividend” check to all American adults last month during the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas. He made it contingent on the GOP winning the midterm elections and said it had to be spent in the U.S.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said he would introduce legislation to support the $5,000 dividend.

“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election … because Republicans (and America) will win!” Moreno wrote on X after Trump made the initial announcement.

On Monday in Kansas, Trump told the audience he’ll make the sale of E15 — fuel blended with 15 percent ethanol — allowed year-round instead of being restricted during the summer months for environmental reasons, but only if GOP Sen. Roger Marshall wins reelection next month.

He said more “goodies” could be coming if the Republicans in Kansas are elected.

In North Carolina on Tuesday, Trump tied Camp Lejeune toxic water settlements to the GOP winning.

“If we don’t win, there’s no money,” he said in Greenville. “If we do win, you’re getting it. It’s going to be finally over with that nightmare that’s been going on for so many years. We will never abandon the heroes who served America.”

Last week in Kentucky, he promised a major investment of $100 million in the pharmaceutical company Antheia to revitalize the facility if Republicans win.

He said Ohio would be “very strongly” considered for the Space Force Academy if Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) prevails over Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown.

Trump has also promised millions in disaster relief to states like Iowa, Kentucky and Wisconsin, all contingent on the Republican candidates winning.

Some have called Trump out for these conditional promises.

“Wisconsinites will believe it when we see it,” Democratic Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers wrote on X about Trump’s promise of disaster aid to Wisconsin if Republican candidate Tom Tiffany wins.

“Clearly, President Trump and Congressman Tiffany are continuing to play politics with emergency aid that’s meant to help communities recover in the wake of disasters like tornadoes and floods,” he wrote. “That’s Complete and Total Bulls—.”

Trump’s approval rating hit a record low in a new Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released over the weekend, at 33 percent. Roughly 66 percent said they disapprove of his performance.

High costs and the Iran war have hurt Republicans and made them wary of their elections.

“We’re facing an extraordinarily cynical electorate,” Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow in Governance Studies at the Brookings Institute, said. “So it’s hard to imagine that any of this works.”

Questions of legality have arisen, especially surrounding the $5,000 dividend Trump promised to Americans if Republicans win.

“In a lot of ways, the way the Trump administration and Donald Trump himself, the way they sort of propose things and they talk about money and politics often is very crass because it’s obviously what they are trying to incentivize people to do,” Kang said. “But in other ways I think the Trump’s administration and Trump himself, they’re very clever about just saying things in a way that avoids the kind of legal problems.”

Richard Briffault, a professor at Columbia Law School, said Trump’s promises are “constitutionally protected messages…they’re constitutionally protected speech.”

“It doesn’t really amount to the level of bribe because he’s not offering anything to any one person,” Briffault said. “I think it’s the sheer implausibility of it that takes it out of any kind of legal or ethical setting and basically makes it into empty campaign rhetoric.”

And Kamarck said she doesn’t see these promises getting Republicans extra votes.

“He’s desperate and so he keeps…taking spaghetti, throwing it against the wall and see what sticks,” Kamarck said. “He’s throwing out things to see if any of them could convince Americans to vote for Republicans in the midterms. And I don’t think it’s going to work.”

“This is totally unprecedented for presidents,” she said of the promises.

articles.title: GOP pushes for oversight of Musk’s dominance of space
articles.summary: Republican lawmakers alarmed over Ukraine’s loss of access to Starshield, a critical battlefield tool, are pushing for more congressional oversight on what some view as Elon Musk’s “space monopoly,” fearing that Musk will have too much power over future national security operations. Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, on…
articles.body:
Republican lawmakers alarmed over Ukraine’s loss of access to Starshield, a critical battlefield tool, are pushing for more congressional oversight on what some view as Elon Musk’s “space monopoly,” fearing that Musk will have too much power over future national security operations.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, on Thursday said he’s concerned that U.S. national security has become overly reliant on Musk and his company, SpaceX, which owns Starlink and its military-oriented division Starshield.

Cramer visited the Senate’s secure compartmented information facility, or SCIF, to get a classified update on Ukraine’s loss of access to Starshield.

He expressed “concern” that “we’re putting too many eggs in one company’s basket when it comes to our space assets.”

He said he would appeal to Republican leadership that “we pour a lot of resources … into making sure there’s a lot of competition both for satellite production and satellite launch.”

Cramer said SpaceX has too much of a stranglehold on the commercial space industry and expressed concern that it could have major future implications for U.S. national security.

Cramer said he has significant concern that Musk “has as much power as he does as one individual and one company over America’s ability to protect the domain of space, which is a warfighting domain.”

A Senate Republican aide, who requested anonymity to comment on the sensitive topic, confirmed it’s “a concern” that Musk’s SpaceX has become too dominant.

Musk’s dominance over space operations was crystalized in March 2025 when NASA needed a SpaceX dragon capsule to rescue astronauts Suni Williams and Butch Wilmore, who had been stranded for 286 days on the International Space Station because of a critical propulsion failure suffered by Boeing’s Starliner, which was originally scheduled to pick up the crew.

There’s growing tension in the space policy world between legacy contractors such as Boeing and new commercial space ventures such as SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin.

Blue Origin is trying to accelerate its heavy space launch program, but it still lags Musk and SpaceX, congressional sources say.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth appeared to point some blame at Musk on Wednesday for Ukraine’s restricted access to Starshield last week.

Rubio told reporters Ukraine’s access to Starshield is “governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at.”

Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), the former chair of the House Intelligence Committee, over the weekend called for an investigation into who was responsible for limiting Ukraine’s access.

“There needs to be an investigation. We need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things,” he told CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

Four Republican senators, Sens. John Cornyn (Texas), Thom Tillis (N.C.), Susan Collins (Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), signed on to a bipartisan letter last week calling on the Defense Department’s inspector general to investigate whether senior Pentagon officials had any role in limiting Ukraine’s access to Starlink or Starshield.

Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.) also called for an investigation after The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered the slowdown of Ukraine’s access to Starshield.

“We got to call the witnesses, got to bring them in, put them under oath, and get to the bottom of it,” he said Tuesday. “We cannot just move past this. This is a serious, serious issue because lapsing Starshield in that manner that costs human lives, there’s got to be consequences to that.”

Ross Gerber, a SpaceX investor, told CNN in an interview that the decision to restrict Ukraine’s data speeds on Starshield has “given everybody a reason not to use Starlink,” adding that “Starlink isn’t reliable for national security for anybody but Trump.”

At the same time, some NATO allies are now asking whether they can continue to rely on SpaceX to provide essential battlefield communications during a conflict.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski suggested the prospect of Musk “playing politics” with a vital national security-related technology is giving European governments reason to reconsider it as a pillar of their defense communications networks.

“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” he warned on the social platform X, which Musk also owns.

The growing GOP scrutiny of Musk’s power over the future of U.S. space operations sets the stage for bipartisan action in the next Congress as several influential Democrats, such as Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.), say that Musk’s power needs to be reined in.

Warren, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, this week called for an investigation into who ordered the limit on Ukraine’s access to Starshield and warned of an “enormous risk” if Musk is “dictating our foreign policy” by having control of Ukraine’s ability to use its drones and other military aircraft.

“We’d like to know exactly who is responsible for what happened,” she told CNN. “If it is one man, Elon Musk, who is dictating our foreign policy, then he puts the United States at enormous risk.”

Warren called for an investigation of Musk and Starlink two years ago in response to a report that Musk had curbed a Ukrainian military operation that intended to strike Russia’s naval fleet in the Black Sea.

Some Republicans are predicting that Democrats will push hard to rein in Musk’s federal contracts if they win control of the House, and possibly the Senate, in next month’s election.

“Musk is in for a rude awakening,” warned a GOP aide.

articles.title: The Memo: Trump backs controversial Ohio ad, pouring fuel on midterm campaign fires
articles.summary: President Trump intensified the furor over a deeply controversial political ad on Thursday, backing the decision by the GOP’s gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy, to run the commercial. In doing so, Trump poured fresh fuel on a bitter midterm campaign that has seen the president deride the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan, Abdul…
articles.body:
President Trump intensified the furor over a deeply controversial political ad on Thursday, backing the decision by the GOP’s gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy, to run the commercial.

In doing so, Trump poured fresh fuel on a bitter midterm campaign that has seen the president deride the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, as a “jihadist”; use an anti-trans slur against Annie Andrews, the Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina; and habitually refer to James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, as “Talafreako.”

Trump has also referred to El-Sayed by his middle name, Mohamed, in a way that critics contend is a clear appeal to Islamophobia. The tactic has drawn parallels with Trump’s long record of seeking to “other” former President Obama by repeatedly invoking his middle name, Hussein.

Trump has shot back over El-Sayed, contending that, as president, “I can call him whatever the hell I want.”

At a Wednesday rally in South Carolina, Trump again used a slur against Andrews, referring to her as “Tr—y Annie.” Andrews is not trans.

Asked to respond to general criticism of Trump’s campaign trail rhetoric, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told this column via email: “President Trump doesn’t care about being politically correct, he cares about Making America Great Again. The American people love how authentic, transparent, and effective the President is, which is why he won in a massive landslide victory on November 5, 2024.”

Ingle also contended that, in relation to the midterms, the choice facing voters is between “doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”

For the moment, however, it is the Ramaswamy ad that is dominating the national political conversation.

The ad centers upon Donna Arthur, the long-estranged mother of Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

In Acton’s telling, an extremely troubled childhood included repeated sexual abuse by her stepfather. Her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was charged for sexual conduct with a minor, and initially pleaded not guilty. He later fled the state with Acton’s mother before he could face a full trial. He died in 2004.

In the ad, Arthur calls her daughter a “liar” with a “serious problem.”

The commercial has caused a firestorm. Even though family members have sometimes appeared in negative political ads before, it’s a rare occurrence — and none has had the deeply traumatic backstory of the Acton matter.

Several Republicans have been critical of the ad, including Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R).

DeWine, who is leaving office due to term limits, said running the ad was “wrong” and called the commercial “deeply troubling.” Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who is in a tight race with Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown, has said he would not have run the ad. Former Ohio Gov. John Kasich (R) also condemned the ad, saying during an MS NOW interview on Thursday that “there is nothing appropriate” about the commercial.

“The reaction to all of this has been disgust,” Kasich added.

That has not been the reaction at the highest levels of the Trump administration, however.

Vice President Vance, who previously served as a senator representing Ohio, told reporters on Wednesday that his disgust was focused on those Republicans “who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America.”

Then, Trump weighed in with a lengthy social media pos t on Thursday in which he praised the ad as “very powerful,” and disparaged DeWine as someone who “probably” wants the Democrat to win the race.

“The Press is trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it’s so good! Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt,’” Trump continued.

Speaking on Thursday afternoon with reporters, Trump implied he was not aware of Acton’s descriptions of childhood abuse. According to pool reports, the president insisted, “I don’t know what the daughter said.”

More broadly, Republicans have hit out at the language used by some Democrats as the midterm campaign hits its final stretch, though those instances have been generally less visceral and personal than Trump’s attacks.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who is not running for reelection this year, sparked controversy with comments at the University of Chicago last week because of the way she said her party should use its oversight powers if it won control of Congress.

Slotkin said: “I want young people coming out of school to say, ‘Should I go work for the Trump administration?’ … I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want. And so let me avoid participating in that.’ I want that deterrence message sent.”

Republicans contended Slotkin was trying to intimidate young conservatives out of taking on a more active role in politics. Her defenders countered she was merely arguing that wrongdoing should incur consequences.

The Democratic Senate candidate in Maine, Troy Jackson, also drew criticism for telling his Republican opponent, Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during a debate earlier this month.

Republicans also object to the language used by prominent Democrats about Trump and his allies generally.

An official account allied with California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) called White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller a “fascist cuck” last year, for example. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) was widely seen as using sexual innuendo when he referred to Trump and White House aide Natalie Harp at a rally over the summer.

Those moments have cut both ways, however. The vice president was just as widely criticized for insinuating that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is gay at a rally earlier this month.

It’s not exactly the Lincoln-Douglas debates.

But Ryan Skinnell, an expert in political rhetoric and a professor of rhetoric and writing at San José State University, noted that the explosion of social media — and its often cruder sensibilities — is part of the picture.

“In a long history of media, this kind of thing happens basically whenever there is a new medium that pops up. You can see versions of this increasing extremism after the invention of radio, or TV, or even the pulp press,” he said.

At the same time, Skinnell made clear he does not see that historic pattern as exculpatory of those who engage in inflammatory rhetoric — like Trump.

“When he feels threatened. his rhetoric gets more extreme and more aggressive,” Skinnell said of the president.

“When there is a breaking news story that makes him look bad, all of a sudden we see him making really extreme claims. Coming in to an election, the same thing. It’s an attempt to distract from issues like the rising cost of gas. If you say something wildly xenophobic about Abdul El-Sayed, maybe people will get distracted.”

Todd Belt, a professor in the Political Management program at the George Washington University, also highlighted Trump’s rhetoric — but noted it was part of a bigger picture.

“There is a coarsening of our political dialogue,” Belt said. “Over time, we have made politics into more of a bloodsport.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: We analyzed Judge Reyes’s record in Trump cases. Here’s what we found
articles.summary: The Trump administration wants to boot U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes from the battle over East Potomac Golf Links, insisting she has shown open hostility. President Trump called her a “crazed lunatic” on social media. The appointee of former President Biden has been assigned nearly a dozen lawsuits challenging major Trump administration actions, The Hill’s…
articles.body:
The Trump administration wants to boot U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes from the battle over East Potomac Golf Links , insisting she has shown open hostility.

President Trump called her a “crazed lunatic” on social media.

The appointee of former President Biden has been assigned nearly a dozen lawsuits challenging major Trump administration actions, The Hill’s analysis of the judge’s docket shows.

It is true that Reyes has sided against the president on other issues. But she hasn’t always given plaintiffs what they’ve asked for.

Here’s how her record actually stacks up:

In February, Reyes blocked then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem from ending temporary protected status (TPS) for Haitians, only to be overruled by the Supreme Court.

TPS protects foreign nationals who cannot safely return to their home countries because of armed conflict or other temporary conditions. It prevents deportation and provides recipients with a pathway to work authorization. The administration said the program had been abused and had looked to cut off most of the 17 participating countries.

Reyes found that Noem’s revocation of Haiti’s status was likely motivated by anti-Black animus, pointing to how Trump called the nation a “s—hole” country, among other comments.

“Whatever the context and at whatever level of sensitivity one considers them, the statements are what they are: unmitigated expressions of animus towards nonwhite foreigners,” Reyes wrote at the time .

The Trump administration took her ruling all the way to the high court and won.

In a 6-3 decision along ideological lines, Justice Samuel Alito said the TPS statute barred Reyes from considering many of the challengers’ arguments. As for the animus argument, Alito said that was likely to fail, too.

“None of the cited statements by either the President or the Secretary was overtly racial,” Alito wrote.

DHS office closures: Ruled in Trump’s favor

Reyes never stopped the administration when a human rights group sued in the early months of Trump’s presidency over the planned closures of three DHS offices focused on individual liberties.

Reyes declined to issue an injunction after the administration reversed its plans. The human rights group kept pushing, raising concerns that one of the offices was still not carrying out its responsibilities, but the judge refused to intervene.

The parties have now indicated they’re working toward a potential settlement to close out the case.

Transgender troops ban: Ruled against Trump

The Trump administration is currently asking the Supreme Court to review Reyes’s block of the Pentagon’s ban on openly transgender troops serving in the military.

Reyes — who oversees two lawsuits against the policy — blocked it universally in the early weeks of Trump’s presidency. An appeals court limited her ruling so that the Pentagon can implement its policy for new recruits, but it still can’t do so for existing troops. Trump wants the Supreme Court to overrule Reyes entirely.

The justices are on track to consider taking up the administration’s appeal at a closed-door meeting later this term.

“The contrary conclusions of the courts below are irreconcilable with this Court’s precedents governing military deference and gender-identity discrimination,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the administration’s petition filed in August.

The Supreme Court already handed the government a win last year by temporarily agreeing to lift a Seattle-based judge’s block on the ban. Now, the battle is back, this time in Reyes’s case.

D.C. police takeover: Almost ruled against Trump

In August 2025, Reyes was assigned District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb’s (D) lawsuit that challenged the administration’s takeover of the city’s police force.

Trump had declared a crime emergency to assert control of the force as he separately deployed National Guard troops into the city, which remain today.

Reyes hastily scheduled a hearing. She was on the cusp of declaring that the administration had unlawfully taken command when the Justice Department agreed to back off the takeover.

D.C. dropped its case, so officially, the judge never ruled on the city’s arguments.

Inspectors general: Ruled in Trump’s favor

Trump fired inspectors general at various government agencies in the first week of his second term without notifying Congress, as required by law.

Eight of them quickly sued, and their case went to Reyes. She spent nearly six months working on her decision.

The judge ultimately agreed Trump violated the law, but she found she had no power to reinstate the inspectors general. In an opinion invoking the Watergate scandal, she repeatedly criticized Trump.

“They deserved better from their government. They still do,” Reyes wrote.

Iranian immigrants: Ruled in Trump’s favor

In July, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund sued the State Department and DHS over what it says is a policy of providing the Iranian government with information on Iranian nationals seeking asylum in the U.S. It wants to block the sharing.

Reyes declined the group’s request for an immediate injunction after a hearing earlier this month.

The Justice Department is expected to mount an effort to dismiss the lawsuit in the coming weeks.

Reyes oversees one of two lawsuits filed by Mary Comans, the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) former chief financial officer who was fired last year.

Comans was terminated after she distributed roughly $59 million to New York City under a federal grant program that provides funds for housing migrants. The city faced controversy for using the funds for hotel rooms for the individuals.

Reyes hasn’t yet ruled on the government’s effort to toss the lawsuit. Meanwhile, another judge who is overseeing Comans’s other suit issued an order formally clearing her name last week.

Airline labor mediator firing: Suit dropped

Deirdre Hamilton’s challenge to her firing from the National Mediation Board last October also went to Reyes’s chambers.

The board works out labor disputes in the sensitive airline and railroad industries.

Federal law required Trump to have valid cause to fire Hamilton. But similar to his firings at other independent agencies across the government, Trump didn’t claim to have cause.

Instead, he argued the firing protections violate the separation of powers, saying he should be able to sack those officials at will.

Reyes put Hamilton’s suit on hold as the Supreme Court looked at the issue in a separate case, which involved the Federal Trade Commission.

After the justices endorsed Trump’s theory and cast aside a 91-year-old precedent that laid the groundwork for the firing protections, Hamilton voluntarily dropped her lawsuit two weeks later.

It wasn’t the only suit on which Reyes never ended up ruling.

The judge was set to handle three organizations’ challenge to a new Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) policy revoking the 30-day notification requirement before federally subsidized tenants can be evicted.

HUD subsidizes several million households, and the groups said the change was unlawful and could put recipients at risk.

Reyes had set a March 24 hearing to listen to their arguments. But beforehand, HUD indefinitely delayed the new policy — saying it now just a proposal — and the groups dropped their case.

articles.title: Trump sidelines sweeping Russia sanctions as GOP allies warn pressure on Putin is slipping
articles.summary: Trump waived most new Russia sanctions from the Graham Act, drawing sharp Republican criticism over whether Vladimir Putin believes the threats.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is holding back on sweeping new economic penalties Congress handed him to squeeze Russia. He is betting that keeping those sanctions in reserve will help bring Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table, a strategy drawing criticism from Republican allies amid questions about whether Moscow believes he will ever use them. Over roughly a week, the administration waived most of the new Russia sanctions and tariffs enacted last month while separately easing restrictions on Russian diesel exports, moves one foreign policy expert described as Trump's most significant effort yet to unwind economic pressure on Moscow. "It's probably the biggest effort that the Trump administration has made to start unwinding the U.S. sanctions architecture that's been in place against Russia since 2022 or even earlier in some cases," Hal Brands, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, told Fox News Digital. TRUMP TRIES DIFFERENT APPROACH WITH RUSSIA TO BRING AMERICANS RELIEF AMID ONGOING WAR WITH UKRAINE Trump argues that imposing the new penalties could drive Russia away from peace negotiations. But Brands said repeatedly holding back economic punishment risks convincing Putin that Washington is unwilling to follow through on its threats. "The threat of imposition may lose some credibility if over a period of time you've demonstrated that you would prefer not to impose those penalties in the first place," Brands said. REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS BREAK WITH TRUMP ON DIESEL DEAL WITH RUSSIA The decision has drawn criticism from Republicans who helped advance the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, including Trump allies who worked with his White House to pass it. Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., who played a leading role in passing the legislation and joined Trump in the Oval Office when he signed it last month, said Tuesday the administration should be turning up economic pressure on Moscow. "It is my belief that we need to use economic firepower to help drive Putin to the table," Britt told Semafor. "I believe that Russia is at the darkest point that they've been at in this entire war, and now is the time for us to turn up the pressure." Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., said Congress had coordinated the legislation's timing with the White House, making Trump's decision to waive most of its new penalties particularly surprising. "This was an act of Congress that we had worked with the White House on," Capito said. "We had timed this to when the president and the White House felt it was a good time to move forward with this, where it could be effective." Other Republicans were more blunt in their criticism. "Beyond irresponsible," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., wrote on X. "What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day," he added. Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the lead sponsor of the legislation named for her late brother and a Trump-endorsed candidate, said she would "choose to keep the pressure on Russia" because "I don't trust Putin and I don't trust Russia." The Graham Act, signed into law in September, provided for steep tariffs targeting Russia and major purchasers of Russian energy, along with sanctions on Russian financial institutions and foreign entities doing significant business with them. Congress also included presidential waiver authority, which Trump invoked to put most of the law's new Russia penalties on hold. Brands said including a waiver was not necessarily a mistake, even if it ultimately allowed Trump to avoid imposing the penalties lawmakers had sought. "It's really tough to craft a sanctions or tariffs bill that forces the president to do something, and typically you don't want to do that because there are always circumstances one can imagine in which you might want to be able to waive sanctions," he said. Trump has defended his decision as necessary to keep Putin at the negotiating table. "My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote Sunday. In his formal certification to Congress, Trump said imposing the Graham Act penalties now "would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace." He left open the possibility of imposing them later to "incentivize resolution" of the war. Brands acknowledged that holding sanctions in reserve can give a president bargaining power, but questioned whether Putin believes Trump is prepared to follow through. "The challenge is that it's been clear for about 18 months now, since Lindsey Graham started pushing this bill in the first place in the early parts of 2025, that the president simply doesn't have much appetite for squeezing the Russian energy export system to the degree that people like the late Senator Graham envisioned and desired," Brands said. The administration has separately eased existing restrictions to allow more Russian diesel onto the market, a move intended to relieve pressure on global fuel prices. Trump has criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, arguing they are straining diesel markets. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has described sanctions relief as a "carrot" that could encourage Russia to de-escalate. Brands said the immediate financial benefit to Moscow from diesel relief is probably "fairly marginal." The more consequential decision, he argued, was Trump's refusal to activate the broader sanctions and tariffs Congress authorized. "There's a potential for pretty serious pressure to be exerted if he had used both the sanctions authorities and essentially the secondary tariff authorities to go after purchasers of Russian energy products overseas," Brands said. Such measures could "put a fairly significant squeeze on the Russian war economy" while discouraging other countries from doing business with Moscow, he added. Brands acknowledged that squeezing Russian energy exports could further strain global energy markets when Trump is focused on lowering fuel prices at home. But he argued that the larger risk lies in what Putin concludes about Washington's willingness to sustain economic pressure. "Putin's theory of victory in Ukraine for a long time has been that at some point the West, particularly the United States, will get tired of the costs of confrontation with Russia and support for Ukraine," Brands said. The concern, he explained, is less about the immediate revenue Moscow gains from additional diesel exports than the possibility that easing restrictions reinforces Putin's belief that Washington is growing tired of confronting Russia. "The risk you run here has less to do with the precise dollar or ruble amount that Russia will gain by being allowed to export some additional diesel than with the strategic signal you're sending that, in fact, the U.S. is getting tired of applying economic pressure against Russia and that the U.S.-Ukraine relationship is entering another period of conflict and divergence," Brands said. Brands sees little prospect for a negotiated settlement in the immediate future and argued that changing Putin's calculation would require convincing him that the costs of continuing the war outweigh the potential gains. "I think the only way you get there is by continuing to support Ukraine so it can take an increasing toll on Russia on the battlefield and by finding ways of ramping up rather than ramping down the economic pressure on Russia," Brands said. Trump's waiver does not eliminate sanctions against Russia that predated the Graham Act, and the administration can revisit the new penalties. articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Chris Hayes had Ilhan Omar in the hot seat — and failed to ask these 10 questions
articles.summary: Chris Hayes on MS NOW laughed through immigration fraud questions and never pressed Ilhan Omar on DNA evidence, her birth name or marriage claims.
articles.body: "I am trying to figure out the way to do this." Those words from MS NOW's Chris Hayes say all you need to know (and likely all you will get) from his interview on Wednesday with Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota. There is a litany of questions the liberal host never asked of Omar. Those questions have only increased over the years, leading to the current criminal investigation into immigration fraud. At points, Hayes sounded more like a supplicant than a journalist given his discomfort with asking pressing questions. ILHAN OMAR IS NOT THE MINNESOTA CONGRESSWOMAN’S 'REAL NAME': SOURCES The interview had the journalistic nutritional content of a Slurpee that would give any liberal a sugar high and any non-liberal a stomachache. Many of us have stressed that these allegations are unproven, and that little evidence has been confirmed to support the underlying criminal charges. However, I have also written that Omar has been remarkably unforthcoming in rebutting the allegations or providing her own exculpatory information. Instead, she has spent years denouncing the allegations as racist or Islamophobic without addressing the specific claims. HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’ While the Biden administration began aspects of these investigations years ago, Omar again sat for another prolonged interview without being pressed (beyond cursory questions) about long-standing allegations. Hayes exhaustively explored Omar's feelings and reactions to the recent search while largely avoiding any detailed questions about the very allegations that a Washington, D.C., judge found sufficient to show probable cause of criminal conduct. ILHAN OMAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'PAYCHECK TO PAYCHECK' AS DOJ PROBES FINANCIAL DISCLOSURES It may be useful to consider 10 questions not asked of Ilhan Omar. Asking these questions is not to assume that the underlying claims are true, but to establish the facts from Omar's perspective. Immigration fraud It took 12 minutes for Hayes to mention immigration fraud, and he did so by asking her, "How seriously do you take it?" He then prefaced the fraud question with a laugh, saying, "I am trying to figure out the way to do this that doesn't sound like I'm insane." Hayes then laughed further with Omar about questions of marriage fraud and said, "There are right-wing people who believe" these allegations, after Omar agreed that such questions are "insane." Hayes made a series of statements about how "there is not even a kernel of truth" to these claims before inviting affirmations from Omar. He then made a general reference to "moving on to other allegations" without any details. ILHAN OMAR ISSUES STUNNING ADMISSION WHEN CONFRONTED WITH BROTHER MARRIAGE RUMORS The questions not asked: ILHAN OMAR RAID SPARKS OMINOUS PREDICTION FROM WATCHDOG: 'THEY PROBABLY GOT THE GOODS' Financial fraud In the interview, when Hayes moved on to Omar's previous financial disclosure that she and her husband were worth $30 million before dropping to a little over $100,000, he again failed to address allegations that the drop in income was due to fraud. Instead, he asked about her "lifestyle," then moved on to ask what it is like to be one of the least wealthy members of Congress. Questions not asked: If Omar had answered them, any of these questions would have produced a scoop, but that was clearly not the purpose of this interview. Instead, Hayes spent more time asking Omar how she felt about former President Barack Obama defending her than asking about the specific fraud allegations she faces. Hayes culminated the interview by asking, "Do you ever just want to tap out?" and Omar congratulated him on reaching the "real question."
