articles.title: Is ‘gentle parenting’ just a fast way to ruin your child?
articles.summary: We have seen that authoritative parenting works; we know a lot less about gentle parenting.
articles.body:
My parents love my brother and me very much, and they show it constantly. They are the opposite of cold people. Nothing I am about to say should be read as a complaint about affection. They believed that love was most essential — and also that limits and discipline were both part of the job. They did not seem to believe there was any conflict between the two.

My brother and I did not talk back, negotiate or say no to our parents. I am not sure the word “no” was legally available to us. My brother calls our father “Sir.” We helped around the house because that was simply what we did. We never received an allowance.

So I was naturally curious, but also skeptical, when I heard my husband repeat some popular lines about “connection before correction” when it comes to our one-year-old son’s future parenting experience. This phrase is one of the mantras of what people call “gentle parenting.” So I did what any reasonable academic, wife or new mother would do — I opened some books.

The most influential framework for parenting comes from psychologist Diana Baumrind, who in the 1960s sorted parenting along dimensions of warmth and demands. Maccoby and Martin added a fourth style — neglectful or uninvolved parenting — in 1983. The result is the familiar four-part typology for parenting: authoritative , authoritarian, permissive, and neglectful.

The pattern across the meta-analyses is very consistent. A 2018 review found that an authoritative parenting style, emphasizing both responsiveness and making demands of children, is superior in fostering higher academic performance and less negative psychological outcomes.

A second-order meta-analysis of 22 earlier reviews found that only authoritative parenting — not authoritarian, neglectful, or permissive — was positively associated with children’s academic outcomes. By definition, authoritative parenting has warmth but also strict boundaries. A parents practicing authoritative parenting “shapes, controls, and evaluates” children’s behavior “based on the absolute set of standards.” Children do not give input — they are told what to do, and if they don’t do it, there are clear consequences.

However, authoritative parenting is also very warm and loving. It’s just that it’s not a limitless hug. It has structure where the warmth and the limits come as a package deal.

The same body of research points to the other side of the ledger as well: In a meta-analysis of more than 1,400 studies , Martin Pinquart found that harsh discipline and psychological control were the biggest predictors of a child’s behavior worsening over time.

It is clear that warmth without limits is not the answer, but neither is control without warmth. The obvious key is to marry the two. This all validates my own ideas about parenting, but I must admit, there are some uncomfortable elements from my perspective. For example, almost no one has studied gentle parenting directly in spite of its apparent popularity.

The first systematic study, by Alice Davidson and Annie Pezalla, published in 2024 , surveyed 100 parents of children aged two to seven. It offers a useful first look, but it is a look at parents, not children or their outcomes.

Its findings cut in both directions. Inductive analyses identified this approach as one that emphasizes high levels of parental affection and parents’ and children’s emotional regulation. The researchers also found that gentle parenting appears to be distinct from other established measures of parenting approaches in its emphasis on boundaries, but the enactment of those boundaries is not uniform.

In other words, the boundaries are part of the theory, but many parents struggle to hold to them. Overall, gentle parents reported high levels of parenting satisfaction and efficacy, but a subset of gentle parents who were highly critical of themselves reported significantly lower levels of efficacy than the rest of the sample. Statements of parenting uncertainty and burnout were present in more than 33 percent of the gentle-parent sample. That is a finding worth taking seriously.

Here is the main problem: There is no large study that compares children raised with gentle parenting against children raised with the firm-but-warm approach my parents used. The existing research supports a clear statement about warmth and limits, but it does not yet support a clear statement about the label.

So what should we do as parents? My husband and I both agree that the goal is a child who feels understood. But feeling understood and being taught how to function in a world that will not negotiate with you are two different things. A child can only learn the second one if someone is willing to say no.

My own parents didn’t do the worst job in the world, if I do say so myself. My brother and I are not criminals, homeless or even unemployed. Nor have we cut off our family — we actually spend an inordinate amount of time together and with our parents. Our spouses are wonderful, and our parents seem to like them — or at least they say so, which in my family counts as a strong endorsement.

This is anecdote, not evidence. But it is not nothing. I would be a poor scientist if I ignored the single data point I happen to have, but I would also be mistaken to draw sweeping conclusions from it.

So here is my simple conclusion: Gentle parenting is not supported by the data. There are at least some reasons to worry that it might have similar features or outcomes to those of permissive or neglectful parenting. We would have to study that more closely to know for sure, but that hypothesis might be a good place to start.

Warmth is essential and easy to give our child — at least for us. Limits are really essential and sometimes harder to implement. Parents who offer only warmth but treat boundaries as cruelty are not being “gentle” in any meaningful sense that I know of. Rather, they are simply leaving their children to learn life’s hard lessons from people who will be far less kind about it.

Dr. Liberty Vittert Capito is a professor of the practice of data science at the Olin Business School at Washington University in St. Louis.

articles.title: White House blasts Biden border policies ahead of Trump Florida visit, citing brutal hammer killing
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's Fort Myers rally spotlights the brazen hammer killing of a Florida mother by a Haitian national the White House says was released under Biden's border policies.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE – The White House is highlighting the brutal hammer killing of a Florida mother as President Donald Trump prepares to headline a midterm rally in Fort Myers on Friday, with a spokesperson telling Fox News Digital that the case demonstrates the consequences of former President Joe Biden's border policies. Trump is scheduled to speak at 2 p.m. at Florida Gulf Coast University's Alico Arena ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The White House is pointing to the killing in the same city as it prepares to put a spotlight on the president's immigration enforcement record. "A few short months ago, an illegal alien barbarically killed a woman outside of a gas station in Fort Myers by hitting her on the head with a hammer multiple times," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital exclusively. DEM-LED PUSH TO EXTEND PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIANS FACES OUTRAGE AFTER BRUTAL HAMMER KILLING "This heinous murderer was RELEASED into the country by the Biden administration. Not only did the Biden administration release him into the country, but they then gave him Temporary Protected Status. This is the result of Democrats open-border policies. If you import the third world, you become the third world." Trump previously condemned the killing in an April Truth Social post, calling the surveillance video "one of the most vicious things you will ever see" and blaming the Biden administration for allowing the suspect into the country. "This one killing should be enough for these Radical Judges to STOP impeding my Administration’s Immigration Policies," Trump wrote at the time. The remarks refer to the brazen killing of a Florida mother in April. Haitian national Rolbert Joachim is accused of repeatedly striking the woman in the head with a hammer outside a Fort Myers gas station. ICE-LED FLORIDA OPERATION NETS 500 — INCLUDING ILLEGAL ALIENS ACCUSED OF MURDER, CHILD ABUSE, CARTEL TIES According to the Department of Homeland Security, surveillance video showed the suspect smashing the woman's windshield before approaching her and repeatedly striking her in the head with a hammer in broad daylight. The victim, a gas station clerk and mother of two teenage daughters, died in the attack. Fort Myers police enlisted Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to help locate Joachim, who was subsequently arrested on Mango Street, DHS said. The department said Joachim entered the United States in August 2022 and was released into the country under the Biden administration. A federal judge issued a final removal order against him that year, but he later received Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which expired in 2024. The designation allows eligible foreign nationals from certain countries to remain and work temporarily in the United States because of conditions in their home countries. It does not provide permanent residency. TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94% The White House is putting a spotlight on the case as Trump prepares to address supporters in southwest Florida, a region that has delivered strong election results for the president. Trump carried Florida in all three of his presidential campaigns, expanding his statewide winning margin from roughly one percentage point in 2016 to more than 13 points in 2024. In Lee County, home to Fort Myers, Trump won 63.6% of the vote in 2024, compared with 35.3% for former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to official county election results. The White House says Trump's immigration crackdown has led to 17 straight months without releases at the border and the deportation of more than 3 million people who were in the United States illegally. DHS said in April that ICE had lodged an immigration detainer against Joachim following his arrest and that he would face deportation regardless of the outcome of his criminal case. Prosecutors later announced they would seek the death penalty against Joachim, according to local reporting. articles.title: Ramaswamy’s last-ditch attack shows signs of backfiring
articles.summary: In today’s issue: Democrat Amy Acton‘s chances of flipping the Ohio governor’s race seem to have received a boost as backlash to Republican Vivek Ramaswamy‘s controversial ad featuring her estranged mother keeps growing. Ramaswamy has doubled down in defending the ad, which depicts Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a “liar” and saying she needs “help” as part of a message urging…
articles.body:
Prominent MAHA figure quits administration

Democrat Amy Acton ‘s chances of flipping the Ohio governor’s race seem to have received a boost as backlash to Republican Vivek Ramaswamy ‘s controversial ad featuring her estranged mother keeps growing.

Ramaswamy has doubled down in defending the ad, which depicts Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur , calling her daughter a “liar” and saying she needs “help” as part of a message urging Ohioans to vote against her .

Acton’s campaign and Ramaswamy critics have noted that Acton hasn’t been in touch with her mother since she was 12 years old, after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping Acton. Arthur remained married to the stepfather, and Acton was removed from her mother’s care.

Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted its rating of the race Thursday from “Toss-up” to “Leans Democratic.”

In its analysis explaining the move, the forecaster pointed to a comment from veteran Republican pollster Frank Luntz , who called it a “Hail Mary” from Ramaswamy. Luntz said sometimes these types of moves work.

“However, this seems like an awfully risky and desperate move for Ramaswamy, who has already thrown the kitchen sink at Acton yet appears to be behind,” Sabato’s Crystal Ball said in its analysis.

The controversy has fueled widespread backlash from Democrats and divided Republicans, with some denouncing the ad and others calling on him to continue.

President Trump weighed in on the ad Thursday, urging Ramaswamy to “keep it up” in a post on Truth Social .

“Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor,” he wrote.

That echoes similar comments on Wednesday from Vice President Vance , who said he was “disgusted” by Republicans who have broken with Ramaswamy to call for the ad to be scrapped.

Several notable Republicans have said the ad crossed the line.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) called the spot “deeply troubling” and said the campaign should take it down . He noted, however, he wouldn’t withdraw his endorsement of Ramaswamy over it.

Sen. Jon Husted (R), who is in the midst of a competitive Senate race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), said he wouldn’t have run the ad .

Ramaswamy’s campaign hasn’t shown any signs of folding. The campaign confirmed to The Hill that it’s putting $4 million behind the ad to run online and on TV.

But there’s cause for concern for Ramaswamy beyond the criticism from his own party.

Fundraising has surged for Acton in the days since the ad was released, moving her into second place on the Democratic political donation site ActBlue’s list of top fundraisers.

The Decision Desk HQ polling average shows Acton leading Ramaswamy by about 3.5 points, generally inside the margin of error for most polls. She has opened up a bit more of a lead over the past month.

Still, Sabato’s Crystal Ball acknowledged the hurdles still facing Democrats in a state like Ohio, which has increasingly shifted rightward during the Trump era. Polling has underestimated Republicans in Ohio in the recent past, it noted, though that isn’t to say that’s happening again this year.

Robert Alexander , a professor of political science at Bowling Green State University, told The Hill that he believes this incident will likely make Acton more likeable and makes her story more compelling.

“I t’s probably going to draw some people to learn some things about her and what she’s been able to overcome that they hadn’t seen previously,” he said.

Former Rep. Jim Renacci (R-Ohio) said in a post on the social platform X that Ramaswamy needs to pivot quickly. He said voters don’t necessarily elect the most qualified candidate but the one they like, trust or sympathize with the most.

“You can have the strongest résumé, the best policies, and the most impressive background, but none of that guarantees victory if voters don’t like what they see or hear,” he said. “And when voters believe someone has been treated unfairly, sympathy can become a powerful political force.”

He suggested the consequences could extend beyond the governor race.

“And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well.”

▪ The Hill : The Memo: Trump pours fuel on midterm campaign fires.

Trump invoked the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million aimed at boosting domestic gas and diesel production amid high fuel costs. The law gives the president broad powers to increase the production of resources for national defense purposes.

The Supreme Court ruled that New Hampshire’s top election official can entirely stop voters from using their student IDs as a way to prove their identity when going to the polls to vote in the midterms. A lower judge had ruled officials had improperly gone further than a state law implementing restrictions, but the high court said the judge intervened too close to the election.

The Pentagon announced an initial deal with Lockheed Martin to produce at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets over the next decade. Lockheed will contribute at least $7 billion toward the program, according to the Pentagon, and the company said it aims to produce 156 aircraft each year under the deal.

CANNABIS CONSPIRACY : Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas , one of the top-ranking Democrats in the state, was charged and brought into custody Thursday for allegedly leading a wide-ranging criminal enterprise that distributed large amounts of marijuana and laundered the proceeds.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) charged Lucas and six other defendants, including some of her family members, for their roles in the alleged racketeering conspiracy. The charges include marijuana distribution, money laundering, possession of firearms in furtherance of drug trafficking and wire fraud.

Lucas, who was first elected in 1991, serves as president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate and chairs the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee, which handles the state budget. The DOJ is accusing Lucas of using her political position to insulate the alleged criminal enterprise “from criminal scrutiny and to influence legislation benefiting the enterprise.”

“The charges alleged in this indictment reveal the behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche , who announced the indictment alongside FBI Director Kash Patel at a press conference Thursday.

Lucas surrendered to authorities and made a brief appearance in federal court, before she was released on her own recognizance.

The indictment follows an FBI search in May of Lucas’s local office and of a cannabis store she has a stake. At the time, she characterized the search as an effort to intimidate her.

“I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down,” Lucas said in a statement yesterday.

Though Lucas is not up for election this year, the DOJ typically avoids making any moves that could appear political so close to a midterm election. Blanche rejected the suggestion that politics factored into the indictment, telling reporters, “We don’t do political paybacks.”

▪ The Hill : Rep. Ilhan Omar says raid was trying to ‘freak her out.’

MEANS TO AN END : Calley Means , a senior adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a leading proponent of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement within the federal government, resigned Thursday.

Means announced his departure in a post on X , saying he is leaving with “tremendous respect” for Kennedy and the president, adding MAHA had made more gains in the past two years than ever before.

But Means reportedly left the administration over frustration with delays in the MAHA food agenda. The movement’s base has grown more upset with the administration’s approach to its main goals, such as on vaccines and pesticides.

Means’s sister, fellow MAHA influencer and entrepreneur Casey Means , was Trump’s pick for surgeon general, but the nomination was pulled earlier this year amid opposition to her selection.

▪ The Hill : Most Americans confident in childhood vaccine safety, poll finds.

NO BACKING OFF : Trump administration officials and allies are ramping up their attacks on Politico even after the outlet issued a correction on a story about White House chief of staff Susie Wiles .

Politico had reported that Wiles played a direct role in setting up the hard-hitting interview that former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia had with Fox News host Sean Hannity shortly before Zacharia’s ouster from her role. A White House official clarified to the outlet that Wiles only offered “positive reinforcement” for the booking, and the story now includes a correction stating Wiles’s role was mischaracterized.

“Let me get this straight -@politico published a false story saying the exact opposite of what this now-released story says and their explanatory note says they ‘mischaracterized’ the events?” Scott Kupor , director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, wrote on social media Thursday.

“They constantly peddle false gossip and malicious lies from clueless anonymous sources to demean the Trump Administration,” former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt wrote on social media, calling Politico the “worst outlet in Washington.”

This marks the latest instance of Trump World pushing back on Politico, as the administration last month banned the outlet, along with CNN and MS NOW, from accessing the White House. A federal judge ordered their credentials restored .

▪ The Hill : Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in BBC defamation suit.

DON’T BET ON IT: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth barred all Pentagon staff from placing bets related to military action on prediction market platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi.

In a memo first obtained by CBS News, the Pentagon chief warned that U.S. enemies monitor movements in prediction markets and, “When an American Service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal. ”

Hegseth said violations could result in administrative, disciplinary and “where appropriate, criminal action,” in accordance with federal law or the Uniform Code of Military Justice.

The move comes amid a broader debate over who can regulate prediction markets and whether they constitute gambling. Insiders can read more here from The Hill’s Julia Shapero about the unlikely coalitions forming as the sides dig in for a lengthy legal battle.

The president will travel to Fort Myers, Fla., where he will deliver remarks at 2 p.m. He will then go to Palm Beach for the evening.

PROMISES PROMISES : The president’s list of offerings if Republicans win the midterms is becoming longer and more niche as Election Day approaches.

The Hill’s Mallory Wilson and Julia Manchester report that the promises have become a staple of Trump’s campaign stops in the cycle’s final weeks. He’s said all American citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans maintain their majorities and also dangled investments in specific areas.

“When I say something, I mean it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social about the dividend checks.

The efforts have drawn skeptics who question if the big promises will work or if they’re even legal.

“The problem that Trump faces right now is that no one believes him on ending the war. On lowering prices. On giving away money. None of it,” said a former White House official. “I’m not sure if it is hurting Republican candidates, but it certainly isn’t helping.”

More recently, Trump told a Kansas audience he would make the sale of E15, fuel blended with 15 percent ethanol, available year-round instead of just during the summer months — only if Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) wins. He said more “goodies” would also be coming to Kansas.

He also promised a $100 million investment in a pharmaceutical company in Kentucky and to consider Ohio “very strongly” for the Space Force Academy, if Husted wins.

The promises have raised legal and ethical questions, especially the $5,000 checks. But experts said it doesn’t rise to the level of illegal bribery.

“It doesn’t really amount to the level of bribe because he’s not offering anything to any one person,” said Richard Briffault , a professor at Columbia Law School. “I think it’s the sheer implausibility of it that takes it out of any kind of legal or ethical setting and basically makes it into empty campaign rhetoric.”

REIGNITED : Iran claimed Thursday that its navy struck seven oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, potentially sending tensions back up at a time when energy costs are already heightened amid the conflict.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it hit four tankers that were transferring oil, while three ships hit naval mines that rendered them immobile. If confirmed, the attacks would be the largest single-day incident involving vessels in the strait since the war began in February.

The IRGC warned the U.S. military against continued efforts to move oil tankers through the strait and that it would issue a response directed at U.S. bases in the region.

The claims come as a New York Times report indicated the U.S. and Israel are drawing up plans to potentially resume strikes against Iran following the midterms.

Trump has predicted that Iran will agree to more favorable ceasefire terms after the midterms but has threatened to end the war “the hard way” if necessary.

The State Department ordered the departure this week of nonemergency staff and their families at the U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia as the country continues to take fire from the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen.

A total of 21 states and Washington, D.C., allow voters to register on Election Day for the midterms. Prospective voters unsure of their registration status can visit this website to check.

Four states have less clear-cut rules than the others: Massachusetts, New York, and North Carolina allow same-day registration, but only during the early voting period, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures . articles.title: What did federal agents take from Ilhan Omar’s home?
articles.summary: Federal agents took 17 items including Omar’s phone and her husband’s notebooks.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar said she was “surprised” federal agents took 17 items during last week’s federal raid search of her Washington, D.C. home.

Omar told MS Now that her phone , an old phone, her youngest daughter’s phone, her husband’s notebooks, a camera he received from his uncle and a Somali phrase book for children were seized.

“To walk away with 17 items of, like, 10 that were just notebooks and like old phones was such a bizarre, bizarre thing,” she said.

Attorneys for Omar asked the Justice Department on Friday to immediately return property that agents seized, arguing the search stemming from an immigration fraud investigation was “neither justified nor lawful.”

‘I have to figure out where to move’: Omar

Omar also told MS Now that she feels unsafe in her home after the raid.

“Obviously, I can’t continue to live there,” she said Wednesday in her first interview since the search. “I have to figure out where to move to, because our address has been public, and with the death threats that I deal with, it’s no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids visiting off and on and having people track them.”

Federal authorities are reportedly investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork.

Last week, federal prosecutors issued at least 15 subpoenas as part of the investigation, including subpoenas targeting some of her relatives. Omar‘s older sister, Sahra Noor, was questioned by authorities amid the ongoing criminal probe into the congresswoman, NewsNation confirmed Tuesday.

Omar was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen. She said Wednesday in her interview that she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong.”

Omar has not been charged with a crime. She has maintained she has done nothing wrong.

Reports have suggested investigators are examining Omar’s immigration history and whether she and her late father intentionally provided false information about her birth date on immigration paperwork.

NewsNation’s Leland Vittert reported federal agents collected garbage in hopes of obtaining DNA from Omar and her family before the raid at the Minnesota Democrat’s home in Washington, D.C.

Multiple sources familiar with the probe tell NewsNation that potential DNA evidence is critical to the investigation into Omar. They say the case is broader than the public may assume based on longstanding accusations surrounding her immigration history and marital status.

NewsNation’s Rich McHugh and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: America’s vaccine system is an operations failure waiting to happen
articles.summary: Before changing a national vaccination schedule, policymakers should know whether the system can actually deliver it.
articles.body:
American families are caught between shifting guidance on vaccination schedules and the hard job of keeping everyone healthy. The divide between the vaccine-averse and vaccine-seekers keeps widening, and diseases that were once rare are settling into clusters. Measles alone has produced over 4,600 confirmed U.S. cases this year, with 42 new outbreaks reported in 2026.

America’s vaccine system faces more than a crisis of public confidence. It faces a potential operational breakdown. Changing vaccine recommendations without accounting for manufacturing capacity, supply chains, distribution networks and patient access risks turning uncertainty into shortages, delays and declining vaccination rates.

Trust in healthcare has not recovered from the pandemic, when high-stakes decisions were made with limited and evolving information. Into that trust gap has come a flood of mixed signals. This year’s vaccine guidance arrived late or not at all. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has not issued new COVID-19 or RSV recommendations for the 2026-27 season. Four medical groups have stepped in with their own recommendations .

Families hear advice from multiple sources that often conflict, and they are swimming in uncertainty. There is an important difference between vaccine hesitancy and vaccine uncertainty. A hesitant parent questions whether to vaccinate. An uncertain parent may want to vaccinate but doesn’t know which vaccines are available, whether their child is eligible or where to go. The first problem requires building confidence. The second requires making the system work.

Nowhere is this clearer than in the recent calls to revamp the childhood immunization schedule. In August, an executive order called for the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to be given as three separate shots. The split may or may not be implemented. But the harm is already done. The seeds of doubt about vaccine efficacy have been planted without an accurate account of what splitting would mean for families.

Splitting vaccines is a herculean task. Companies would need to develop, test and win regulatory approval for single-disease versions that do not currently exist in the U.S. No manufacturer sells standalone measles, mumps or rubella vaccines here. Companies would have to rebuild entire production lines.

The work does not end at the factory. Every clinic and pharmacy would face three times as many stocking decisions, each with its own demand-uncertainty. Order too few, and families must wait or be turned away. Order too many and doses are wasted. Each additional product brings more syringes to procure and more cold storage capacity to plan for. A system that already struggles to match supply with demand would be asked to do it three times over, just as demand becomes harder to predict.

Before changing a national vaccination schedule, policymakers should know whether the system can actually deliver it. Using mathematical modeling, optimization and simulation, researchers can evaluate how proposed changes would affect manufacturing capacity, distribution networks, inventory requirements, costs and patient access before those changes are implemented.

These tools can help clinics and health departments decide how much of each vaccine to stock and where to place it when demand is hard to predict. They can also show which gaps in information, whether about availability, eligibility or what vaccination will demand of a family, are most likely to push people toward not vaccinating at all.

This cannot be fixed by any single announcement. But media, healthcare professionals and community workers owe the public three things.

First, they should evaluate operational feasibility before announcing policy changes. Policymakers must consider not only the scientific and public health implications of changing vaccination schedules, but also whether the infrastructure exists to implement those changes. Operations research can help by modeling manufacturing capacity, distribution requirements, costs and patient access. Identifying potential bottlenecks before policies are implemented can prevent avoidable shortages, delays and disruptions.

Second, reduce uncertainty for families. Parents should not have to navigate conflicting recommendations or hunt for which vaccines are available, who is eligible or where to obtain them. They hear that schedules are changing but rarely hear how doses, efficacy and timing are set.

Behind many questions is often a simple request for information or flexibility. Public health agencies, healthcare providers and community organizations must deliver clear, consistent and accessible information and make the vaccination process easier to navigate. Providing flexibility can help ensure that families who want to vaccinate actually can.

Third, build resilience into vaccine supply chains. Changes to vaccination schedules can have consequences throughout the system, from manufacturers and distributors to pharmacies and clinics. Using forecasting, mathematical modeling and optimization, healthcare systems can better anticipate shifts in demand, allocate limited resources, manage inventory and identify vulnerabilities before they become crises.

The goal is not simply to respond to shortages when they occur, but to design a system capable of adapting to changing circumstances and patients’ preferences without compromising access to vaccines.

Americans cannot make informed vaccination decisions if the system designed to deliver those vaccines is unpredictable, confusing or unprepared. Restoring public confidence requires more than clearer guidance. It requires ensuring that the vaccines policymakers recommend are the vaccines manufacturers can produce, providers can deliver and families can actually obtain.

A vaccine policy is only as effective as the system that delivers it.

Leela Nageswaran, Ph.D., is a researcher at the University of Washington.

articles.body:
President Trump said early Friday morning that the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was 85 percent full and “looking really good” after months of a multimillion-dollar renovation project .

The president also alleged in a Truth Social post shared shortly before 1 a.m. that the pool “hasn’t worked properly since 1922.”

“We have cameras set up to stop any potential Vandalism, including the grassed areas, which were destroyed by chemical poisoning with a large, and very inappropriate, phrase,” he continued, referencing a June etching of the numbers “86 97” on the ground near the World War II Memorial, which the Trump administration interpreted as a threat against the president.

Trump added, “The grass was completely replaced!”

Earlier this week, the president announced that security cameras had been installed around the iconic water feature, and he warned potential vandals they could “GO TO JAIL.”

“We are watching very closely, and security cameras have been installed,” Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social . “Reports are that it’s looking beautiful, and will only get better, subject to NO VANDALISM, with time.”

The pool is part of the president’s efforts to remake Washington, D.C. Last October, crews demolished the East Wing of the White House to begin constructing Trump’s ballroom. The president has also pushed to have his name added to iconic landmarks like the Kennedy Center and the U.S. Institute of Peace .

However, shortly after the White House unveiled the newly-renovated pool in June, onlookers began to spot a growth of green algae in the water and the pool’s newly-installed “American Flag Blue” base began to peel. The pool was drained again for repairs.

Trump blamed these problems on alleged vandalism and directed his Justice Department (DOJ) to crack down on alleged culprits. The DOJ later dropped charges against the people accused of vandalizing the pool, including former Olympic canoeist David Hearn.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: 5 House races that will tell the story of 2026

Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!] In all the votes cast for the House of…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ]

In all the votes cast for the House of Representatives in 2024, Republicans won by 2.7 points. In the current average of national House polls, Democrats lead by 9 points. If that average turns out to be predictive, a swing of almost 13 points from the most recent House elections would be a wipeout for the party in power on par with Republican thrashings in 2018 and 2006.

The thoroughly gerrymandered map and the resilience of many incumbent Democrats in their party’s losing 2024 effort means that there aren’t enough competitive seats to produce the massive shifts we’ve seen in other midterm wipeouts, but there are certainly enough to put the Republicans back on their heels in the way they were for the closing years of President Trump ’s first term, or worse.

But we’ve known for a long time that the House had fallen out of play for the GOP. And while House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) cares a great deal about how big his majority is (and how much leverage democratic socialists and Justice Democrats have over his agenda as Speaker), majority size isn’t too important.

But how high the blue wave reaches or how firm the red wall stands will matter to potentially hundreds of races — from the question of control of the U.S. Senate all the way down to local county commissions.

My American Enterprise Institute colleague Camille Miner and I have sorted through the competitive House races to find five — three true toss-ups, one Republican reach and one Democratic reach that, taken together, we think provide a useful snapshot of the 2026 contest overall.

These are the places you can watch on Election Day (Election Week?) to see which way things are running for the rest of the country.

Incumbent: Republican Mike Lawler (elected in 2022)

Republican seat since 2023; 2024 result: Harris +0.6 points

New York’s 17th District covers the rolling hills of the Hudson Valley just north of New York City (Rockland, Putnam and northern Westchester counties). The Republican incumbent, Rep. Mike Lawler , kept his seat in 2024 despite his college blackface photos resurfacing and the district voting for Harris by 0.6 points. The 17th District is a relatively wealthy white suburban area with significant Hispanic and Jewish populations. Lawler positions himself as a moderate despite being endorsed by Trump, and this Wednesday received $500,000 from Elon Musk .

Lawler claims that his competitor Cait Conley was connected to the disastrous Afghanistan withdrawal while she was a counterterrorism official on the Biden National Security Council. Unlike Lawler, however, Conley graduated from West Point and served six overseas deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. Conley ties Lawler’s agenda to Trump’s which is largely unpopular in the district.

Incumbent: Democrat Vicente Gonzalez (elected in 2022)

Democratic seat since 2017 ; 2024 result: Trump +10 (new map)

This is Texas’s easternmost border district. In 2025, the Republican-held state legislature redrew the district to include less of the western edge and more counties up the Gulf Coast, including the southern part of Corpus Christi. The old district was estimated to be 90 percent Hispanic ; the new district will be around 75 percent Hispanic. Despite the district voting for Trump by 5 points in 2024, Rep. Vicente Gonzalez secured some ticket-splitters and won by 3 points over his competitor two years ago. Under the new map, however, the district is more Republican. But whether they vote for the Trump-backed veteran, Eric Flores , will depend a lot on whether the Southern Texas Republican base is motivated to come out and vote.

Republicans understand the weight of this flip as Vice President Vance and Speaker Mike Johnson have both come to rally with Flores. Additionally, many Latino voters who once voted for the president have taken issue with his tariffs and immigration policies and may vote against Republican candidates or not vote at all.

North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District

Incumbent: Democrat Don Davis (elected in 2022)

Democratic seat since 2023; 2024 result: Trump +11.6 (new map)

Encompassing the state’s Inner Banks, North Carolina’s 1st District has now been redrawn to include more rural communities, increasing the Republican population. Trump already won the district in 2024 by 3 points; under the new map he would have won by 11.6 points. The new district has a substantial Black population: 32 percent. But that’s substantially fewer Black residents than the previous map. Democrats cite the change as evidence that North Carolina Republicans are trying to diminish the traditional power of the state’s African American vote. Rep. Don Davis , the incumbent, is the fourth Black Democrat to hold the seat. Before serving in the House, Davis was the mayor of Snow Hill for seven years and spent 12 years in the North Carolina Senate.

His opponent, Laurie Buckhout , is a retired Army colonel who served in Iraq, and was acting assistant secretary of war for cyber policy in the early months of the current Trump administration. This is a rematch from 2024 when Davis beat Buckhout, but Republicans are betting the new district boundaries will be too tough for him. One very modern wrinkle: Buckhout was banned from Kalshi for betting on her own race .

A possible avalanche warning for the GOP

Incumbent: Republican Jeff Hurd (elected in 2024)

Republican seat since 2011; 2024 result: Trump +10

Colorado’s 3rd District is vast. It takes up the entire southern and western parts of the state, including large resort towns like Aspen and Telluride. The majority of residents are white and rural. They voted for Trump by 8 points in 2020 and 10 points in 2024. In October of 2025, Trump gave Rep. Jeff Hurd his “Complete and Total Endorsement of Re-Election.”

However, when Hurd voted to repeal the tariffs Trump placed on Canada, Trump rescinded his endorsement on Truth Social, calling Hurd a “RINO [Republican in name only] Congressman” and going on to endorse the lesser-known challenger and 2020 election denier, Hope Scheppelman .

But Speaker Mike Johnson took issue with Trump’s endorsement pull, and Trump later in another post admitted that he had talked to Scheppelman about serving the country in a “different capacity.” The president then re-endorsed Hurd.

As the district is not as Trump-loving as Trump may think, it is unclear whether the re-endorsement will win Hurd the necessary votes. Hurd’s opponent, Dwayne Romero , is an attractive moderate candidate for many voters. He attended West Point, served as a combat engineer during the Persian Gulf War and was director of the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade under then-Gov. John Hickenlooper (D). Romero has focused his messaging on veterans, public lands, reversing Medicaid cuts and repealing tariffs.

A potential Democratic gerrymandering overreach

California’s 45th Congressional District

Incumbent: Democrat Derek Tran (elected in 2024)

Democratic seat since 2025; 2024 result: Harris +3.9 (new map)

Amid the gerrymandering of Proposition 50 , Orange County was split up, and now the district map resembles a ‘C’ shape instead of the county’s natural circular form. The district is diverse, with an Asian plurality (38.4 percent) and a significant Hispanic and white population as well (30 percent and 25 percent, respectively). But this does not necessarily translate into progressive politics. Many Asian and Hispanic voters still showed up for Trump in 2024.

Rep. Derek Tran beat the Republican incumbent in 2024, in part by criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration policies and foreign relations. Nevertheless, the district still maintains many Evangelical social conservatives and Vietnamese Americans who fear any socialistic policies that harken back to communism. Tran’s competitor Chuong Vo is a former mayor of Cerritos and on the campaign trail has made it very clear that he will fight against socialists in Washington.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Fed timeline challenges reports of migrant baby facing immigration judge alone
articles.summary: ORR officials say the former Acacia Center contract lacked accountability, with redacted invoices totaling over $20 million monthly for legal services.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A federal timeline provided by officials overseeing unaccompanied migrant children challenges reports that a 1-year-old boy was left to navigate immigration court without counsel, showing that legal service providers intervened to secure representation following an initial hearing. Addressing media reports highlighting toddlers appearing before immigration judges, Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) Acting Director Angie Salazar and Senior Advisor John Fabricatori pushed back on headlines alleging systemic gaps in child legal representation, arguing that contractor failures and lack of invoice oversight created the initial court lapses. "We don't have this big movement where we have a bunch of 1-year-olds who are going to court," Fabricatori told Fox News Digital. SEX CRIMINALS, GANG MEMBERS ABUSED CHILD IMMIGRATION PROGRAM TO ENTER US, DHS REVEALS According to ORR timeline records obtained by Fox News Digital, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers first encountered the 1-year-old boy and his 17-year-old mother near Naco, Arizona, on June 25. The child was accompanied by his mother at all court proceedings. The critical gap occurred in July under the agency's former contractor, the Acacia Center for Justice, records show. On July 1, Acacia completed legal orientation and consultation for the mother and child, but failed to file an E28 notice of appearance before the immigration court. Consequently, during the child's first scheduled court hearing on July 8, no attorney was present — not even as a friend of the court — despite Acacia holding an active federal legal services contract at the time. The federal legal services contract with Acacia officially ended July 31. FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME Following the end of the Acacia contract, the agency transitioned legal service oversight to the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI), which officially initiated legal services Aug. 5. During an Aug. 7 appearance, the mother and child were granted additional time to obtain counsel, while USCRI representatives attended subsequent hearings on Aug. 17 and Aug. 28 as a friend of the court. On Aug. 31, a motion was filed by the friend of the court and mother requesting court-appointed counsel at government expense, which was later denied by the immigration judge. Progress continued into September as child advocates were officially appointed on Sept. 23, and USCRI filed a formal E28 notice of appearance on Sept. 25 to become the attorney of record. On Sept. 29, USCRI officially represented both mother and child in immigration court. The judge subsequently granted a continuance on Oct. 2, leading into a follow-up hearing scheduled for Friday. Officials explained that the July breakdowns highlighted the core reason the administration terminated Acacia's multimillion-dollar contract, which was awarded under the Biden administration in November 2023. According to federal contract records on USAspending.gov, the Department of Health and Human Services had awarded the Acacia Center for Justice a $356.3 million bridge contract for legal services for unaccompanied children. Of that total award, more than $236.9 million had been outlaid prior to the contract's dissolution. The network previously provided counsel to roughly 20,000 migrant children across the U.S., according to its website. "I knew we were signing off on every invoice that we were receiving for legal services to the tune of $20-plus million sometimes each month," she told Fox News Digital. "So it made no sense to me that legal service providers were saying kids were unrepresented for a lack of funding." "I tried to understand who was represented before," she added. "I tried to understand what we were paying for under this direct representation, but the invoices we received were completely redacted. There is no way I could ever know exactly what service was provided during the month." Fox News Digital has reached out to the Acacia Center for Justice for comment. The contract funded a slew of services, including legal screenings, representations and presentations on the rights of migrant children in detention. Following the dissolution of the Acacia contract, the ORR entered into a $20 million contract with USCRI, which expires Dec. 31. "So USCRI was showing up in court as a friend of the court to ensure that there was at least somebody present in case Acacia did not show up," Fabricatori said. "Now, as those cases are being looked at, USCRI is able to go in and actually meet with these children and then represent them in a follow-up hearing. So there may be some hearings where a child shows up, and initially they don't have representation, but USCRI will be there, identify that child, and then be able to move forward in the future as a representative for that child." WOMAN EXPOSED RUNNING VISA FRAUD SCHEME SPANNING YEARS, POSING AS IMMIGRATION OFFICER Salazar emphasized that ORR officials track which children are represented by which lawyers on specific dates, noting that the agency respects attorney-client privilege. "The former provider refused to give us those measurables," Fabricatori said. "They refused to give us the alien registration number so we could determine what cases they were actually representing. They didn't want to give that. They refused to give that, and that was a holdup for us because we needed to know who was actually being represented so we can ensure that every kid at least had their legal orientation and had a legal representative that was talking to them." HUNDREDS OF JAILED ILLEGAL ALIENS RELEASED BACK ONTO BLUE-STATE STREETS DESPITE ICE DETAINERS, RECORDS SHOW Salazar noted that about 2% of migrant children in ORR custody are under the age of 5. Another 85% are ages 13 to 17, with 62% falling into the 16-to-17 bracket. "What we said to our new grantee (USCRI): ‘We want you in 100% of the hearings where kids in our care are showing up to their immigration hearings,’" she said. "That is happening. I think we're at like 98%." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fabricatori added there are currently 1,690 migrant children in ORR custody. "Under Biden, they had 22,000 in care a day. So it's a very vast difference," he said. "We've been able to lower that census, get kids through the court process quicker, and get them back with their parents if possible."

articles.title: Trump suggests Omar resign ‘immediately’ over ‘fake name’
articles.summary: President Trump called on Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) to “IMMEDIATELY resign” and accused her of using a fake name in a Truth Social post on Thursday evening. “Please inform the Speaker of the House of Representatives, James Michael Johnson, that the Dumocrat Party has just conceded her seat,” Trump wrote. “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, her…
articles.body:
President Trump called on Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) to “IMMEDIATELY resign” and accused her of using a fake name in a Truth Social post on Thursday evening.

“Please inform the Speaker of the House of Representatives, James Michael Johnson, that the Dumocrat Party has just conceded her seat,” Trump wrote. “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, her real name, has openly admitted to FRAUD, and she will not be legally allowed to be a Member of this August Body from this point forth.”

In a Wednesday court filing a week after federal agents conducted a search warrant of Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., federal prosecutors referred to the Minnesota Democrat as “Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi” without explanation.

Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in Washington D.C., suggested Omar’s name could be part of a federal probe into the lawmaker, during an appearance on Fox News Thursday.

“If you have citizenship in this country, your derivative citizenship, or your naturalization, your application, will turn on precise information, and you have an obligation to report that precise information,” she said.

“So the question is, who is Ilhan Omar, and has she followed all of the laws as it relates to naturalization and immigration.”

The Trump administration is investigating the Somali-born lawmaker for alleged immigration fraud — an accusation she has repeatedly denied. Omar has accused the president of waging a “ campaign of political intimidation ” against her for years.

During an interview with MS NOW’s Chris Hayes on Wednesday, Omar said she would have to move out of her D.C. apartment because of the threats she has received after the federal search, in which she said agents seized 17 items.

The Democratic lawmaker told Hayes she was “confident” that she had done nothing wrong.

“I am a person of enormous faith,” she said. “And I know that … if I continue to live my truth, if I continue to fight for the right things, if I continue to stand up to bullies and people who are carrying out ungodly corruption, I’m going to be OK.”

On Thursday evening, Trump again invoked a conspiracy theory platformed by far-right commentators that Omar had married her brother, claiming they had the same last name. Omar called the accusation “insane” during her interview with MS NOW this week.

The president claimed in his Truth Social post that the Democrat replied to the question about whether she married her brother by saying, “Not to my knowledge.”

Trump added, “In other words, she somehow didn’t know?”

In the interview, the lawmaker made the statement after Hayes pressed her further about whether she was “related to him at all.” The Democrat laughed before adding, “Not to my knowledge.”

Trump also led calls for her removal from Congress during an Iowa rally on Thursday.

“If you get sworn in with a false name, I would imagine that’s pretty tough to remain,” he said, eliciting chants of “Lock her up” from the crowd.

This is not the first time the president has demanded Omar resign. During his first term, Trump requested the Democrat be removed from Congress and be stripped from her congressional committees for comments he called anti-Semitic.

The Hill has reached out to Omar’s office for comment about his latest demands.

articles.title: Musk midterm spending tops $442M
articles.summary: Tech billionaire Elon Musk has spent more than $442 million in the midterm elections, after pouring another $76.8 million into his super PAC over the past month, campaign finance filings show. America PAC, which Musk launched during the 2024 elections, received the influx of cash from the SpaceX and Tesla CEO over the course of…
articles.body:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk has spent more than $442 million in the midterm elections, after pouring another $76.8 million into his super PAC over the past month, campaign finance filings show.

America PAC, which Musk launched during the 2024 elections, received the influx of cash from the SpaceX and Tesla CEO over the course of about a week in October, according to the super PAC’s last filing before the midterms.

This comes on top of the $366 million he had already spent so far on the upcoming elections. He gave a combined $276 million to his super PAC and various Republican groups in the three-month stretch between July and September alone.

Musk has spent heavily backing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) amid a tight race for the Lone Star state’s Senate seat against Democrat James Talarico.

He gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, in two increments in September that were each disbursed to a Texas super PAC backing Paxton a day later.

Musk also gave $10 million to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which is supporting Paxton, in addition to sending $20 million to a House GOP super PAC, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association.

The tech mogul’s massive campaign donations for Paxton drew scrutiny from his opponent, with Talarico accusing Musk on Wednesday of trying to “buy his own personal” senator.

“There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator,” Talarico wrote on the social platform X, which Musk also owns.

Musk, the world’s richest man, is currently worth $909.8 billion, according to Forbes’ Real-Time Billionaires list. He briefly became the world’s first trillionaire earlier this year, when SpaceX made its stock market debut with the biggest initial public offering (IPO) on record.

His spending this election cycle is well above the sum he spent in the 2024 elections, when Musk first jumped into the political world. After spending about $290 million backing President Trump and Republicans, he became a high-profile figure in the administration.

In the first few months of the administration, he led the controversial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which oversaw sweeping cuts to the federal workforce and grants.

Musk ultimately left the administration in late May, shortly after which he engaged in a fierce public feud with Trump. He pulled back from the political sphere, later suggesting he “got carried away” and “a little too involved in politics.”

But he has increasingly appeared at high-profile events with the president in recent months, joining him on a state visit to China this spring alongside other tech executives. He also sat at Trump’s table at the state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping last month and received the National Medal of Science from the president earlier this month.

articles.title: Put the last cell tower in orbit
articles.summary: The FCC should utilize its $9 billion 5G Fund to subsidize direct-to-device satellite service in areas where traditional cell tower construction is impractical.
articles.body:
In a recent report, the Federal Communications Commission revealed a worrisome paradox in America’s cellular networks: they reach nearly everyone, but not nearly everywhere. While 95 percent of the U.S. population can receive 5G service from at least one carrier, only 69 percent of the nation’s road miles and 39 percent of its land area have such coverage. In rural America, the numbers fall to 60 percent and 38 percent.

This is the rural-mobile divide. It is not about whether a household can obtain broadband at home. It is about losing mobile service while driving, farming, hiking, fighting a wildfire or responding to an emergency.

The conventional solution is to build more cell towers. Some are still needed. But extending terrestrial networks to every remote road, ravine and mountaintop would be economically irrational. The FCC has approved a plan to provide up to $9 billion to close the remaining gaps in America’s 5G cellular networks. But instead of treating every dead zone as a construction problem, we should consider whether the last cell towers should instead be placed in orbit.

Technology advances now offer a promising alternative to cover this last and most expensive frontier. Direct-to-device satellite service allows an ordinary compatible cellphone to connect directly to a satellite when no terrestrial tower is available. The satellite effectively becomes a cell tower in space. No satellite phone, dish or other specialized equipment is required.

All three national carriers see satellites becoming an integral part of mobile networks. T-Mobile already offers this service through Starlink . The service is included with some T-Mobile plans and sold for $10 a month per line to other eligible users, including subscribers of competing carriers. AT&T and Verizon have their own satellite partnerships. And in May, all three carriers announced plans for a joint venture to expand direct-to-device coverage, pool spectrum and make it easier for satellite operators to reach their customers.

Direct-to-device satellite service doesn’t replace terrestrial 5G. Its capacity is limited , and initial offerings emphasize messaging, emergency communications and selected low-bandwidth applications. Voice and more capable data services are in development. But even basic connectivity can transform a dead zone into a place where someone can summon help, report an accident or tell family members they are safe.

The question is how to deploy that capability quickly and affordably. The answer begins with the FCC’s 5G Fund for Rural America . Subsidizing cellular services in areas where private investment alone won’t support deployment was originally proposed in the 2010 National Broadband Plan . The FCC established the 5G Fund in 2020, making available up to $9 billion in Universal Service Fund support over 10 years for mobile service in high-cost areas.

The existing rules require fund recipients to deliver conventional 5G speeds that today’s satellite service cannot yet provide. But before committing to a decade of conventional construction, the agency should create a direct-to-device tier to buy basic mobile coverage in places that towers cannot economically reach, then let competing terrestrial-satellite partnerships bid to provide it.

Instead of prescribing the infrastructure carriers must build, the FCC should buy the coverage it wants and let providers compete over how best to deliver it. How would it work? The FCC could ask carriers to bid for the minimum subsidy they need to provide satellite coverage in designated unserved areas without charging the premium. Carriers would receive support only in return for meeting clear requirements for availability, reliability, emergency communications and compatibility with widely used handsets.

That condition would advance the Communications Act’s promise that consumers in rural and high-cost areas should have access to communications services that are “reasonably comparable” to those available in urban areas, at “reasonably comparable” rates.

“Reasonably comparable” doesn’t require identical service or prices. Courts allow the FCC to balance comparability with affordability and responsible stewardship of the Universal Service Fund.

Here, the balance is clear. Spending enormous sums to extend a terrestrial network over the most challenging terrain would drain resources from places where towers remain economically viable. Leaving that terrain uncovered, on the other hand, perpetuates the rural divide. And charging those who most often encounter dead zones an additional $120 a year makes those least well served pay extra for basic connectivity.

The FCC’s rules require recipients of 5G Fund support to offer rural service at rates reasonably comparable to urban rates. Offering the same rates, terms and conditions in urban and rural areas can satisfy that rule. So, extending the requirement to subsidized direct-to-device coverage would be an evolution of existing universal-service policy, not a new system of price regulation.

Universal-service policy has always adapted to changes in network technology and economics. direct-to-device changes both. The last cell tower needed to close the rural divide no longer has to be built on the side of a mountain. It can be deployed in space, using a federal fund already authorized to bring mobile service to remote locations the market cannot economically reach.

Blair Levin is a former chief of staff of the Federal Communications Commission and directed the writing of the 2010 National Broadband Plan. Larry Downes is the co-author of “Big Bang Disruption” and other books on disruptive innovation.

articles.title: Ex-FBI officials charged with lying to Congress about Hunter Biden probe
articles.summary: Two former FBI officials are facing charges for lying to Congress about their involvement in the agency’s investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop. Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, who worked in the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force (FITF) in 2019 and 2020, were taken into custody Friday, FBI Director Kash Patel said in a post on…
articles.body:
Two former FBI officials are facing charges for lying to Congress about their involvement in the agency’s investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop.

Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, who worked in the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force (FITF) in 2019 and 2020, were taken into custody Friday, FBI Director Kash Patel said in a post on the social platform X .

Patel said in his post that both Floris and Benavides testified earlier that the FITF was not involved in the investigations into Biden, but documentary evidence, communications and witness accounts contradict their testimony.

“Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system,” Patel said. “No one is above the law.”

Biden’s laptop was seized by the FBI in 2019 and contained some of his personal information. The contents of the laptop, including emails showing discussions of Biden’s foreign business dealings, were published by the New York Post, which said it had obtained a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Biden at a Delaware repair shop, according to The Associated Press .

In a Friday release , the Department of Justice (DOJ) said the charges stem from an ongoing investigation into the FITF.

The department cited evidence that Floris discussed the FBI’s investigations routinely for more than a year within the FITF and with others in the FBI. Benavides also regularly discussed the laptop investigation with FBI officials.

“The weaponization of government goes against the interest of the American people, and public servants, including federal law enforcement officials, cannot lie to Congress and get away with it,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the DOJ release.

Both Floris and Benavides made their first appearance in federal court in Washington following their surrender Friday, where their lawyers asked for a speedy hearing at which they could contest the allegations, the AP reported .

Floris’s lawyers issued a statement disputing the allegations and calling her “a patriot.”

“Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years,” a statement obtained by The Hill said.

“Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election,” the statement continued.

articles.body:
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and wife to Great Britain’s Prince Harry, has addressed the accusations against her father, who is being investigated over alleged possession of child sexual abuse material.

Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the news concerning 82-year-old Thomas Markle Sr. that has spread through tabloids in recent days. Meghan and her family recently returned to England after forfeiting their royal duties and living in the United States for a number of years.

“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” Meghan wrote in a statement obtained by The Hill.

According to British tabloid The Sun , Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr. told police he found “hundreds if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images in his father’s home. Meghan, who is said to have been estranged from her father for years, said allegations were made to British police in 2018 and were later shared with her.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection,” Meghan wrote. “That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”

The Sun reported that Markle Jr. reported his father to officials after finding the boxes of photos and a 15-minute video of naked young girls on his father’s phone. Markle Jr. reported his father to multiple law enforcement authorities, including the FBI, The Sun reported.

Meghan said in her statement that she trusted the authorities to protect any families at risk while she avoided her father to protect her young children.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” Meghan wrote. “I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

Meghan said she hopes that justice will be served and children will be protected.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan wrote.

articles.body:
A federal appeals court on Friday ruled 2-1 that President Trump’s National Guard deployment to the Los Angeles area last year was unlawful.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit rejected Trump’s assertion that violent demonstrations in the city protesting his immigration crackdown justified him wresting control of the troops from Gov. Gavin Newsom (D).

Although Trump’s deployment has ended, the decision caps a year of consideration by the appeals court.

At an earlier stage of the case, the 9th Circuit sided with Trump . It’s now ruling against him after the Supreme Court similarly found Trump didn’t meet the legal requirements to unilaterally deploy the National Guard to Chicago.

“Defendants have not made either of the required threshold showings here. Thus, they have not carried their burden,” said U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Sung, an appointee of former President Biden.

Sung was joined on the panel by two Trump-nominated judges, Eric Miller and Mark Bennett. Miller also sided against Trump, while Bennett dissented.

Bennett said his colleagues shouldn’t have decided the case, as the administration wanted to dismiss the appeal and head back to the trial court to litigate the impact of the Supreme Court’s ruling.

“But the majority insists on pressing forward, relying primarily on outdated briefs prepared amid a shifting legal landscape,” Bennett wrote.

It means Friday’s decision will now bind future 9th Circuit panels if Trump tries to deploy the National Guard again in California.

Last year, Trump deployed the National Guard to various blue cities around the country — including Washington, Memphis and Portland, Ore. — to quell protests against his immigration crackdown.

In Los Angeles, the demonstrations devolved into violence at times, with reports of looting and some having thrown Molotov cocktails.

The president deployed the National Guard by invoking a law allowing him to federalize troops whenever there is a rebellion or when he cannot execute the law with regular forces.

The Supreme Court last year said Trump hadn’t met the criteria because “regular forces” likely refers to the U.S. military.

Trump’s National Guard deployment in the nation’s capital, which relies on a different legal authority, remains ongoing.

As the race for control of Congress enters its final days, 2WAY is teaming up with NewsNation and The Hill for another special edition of “The Morning Meeting” ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections on Sunday, Oct. 25.

These special midterm editions of The Morning Meeting are presented in partnership with NewsNation and The Hill.

The Oct. 25 program is the second of three special editions leading up to Election Day. Viewers will also have a chance to ask questions and join the conversation live. Those interested in participating must register through 2WAY .
